This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way and potential future directions. Furthermore, the authors identify commonalities between quantum deep learning and pre-trained models in the language domain, noting that similarities may indicate a universal pathway to achieving artificial intelligence. This discussion is informed by the authors' personal experiences and recent developments in the field, culminating in an exploration of potential future applications and challenges within quantum deep learning.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator technology continues to be fundamental in 
high-energy physics (HEP) experiments, where significant progress has been 
made over the past decade in advancing the field. This progress could soon lead 
to upgraded existing facilities, enhancements to facilities still under 
construction (such as PIP-II), well-established proposals, or newly emerging 
ideas like the FCC-ee and future proton intensity upgrade at Fermilab, among 
others. Innovations in RF technology not only contribute to HEP but also extend 
beyond to fields such as nuclear physics, basic energy sciences, and other areas, 
as evidenced by European XFEL, LCLS-II and related facilities, or SHINE, 
EIC, and FRIB. Therefore, an extensive R&D program focusing on RF technology 
is needed to tackle challenges in accelerator-based applications and introduce 
new, promising technologies.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy muon collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

We have determined the dispersion relations for relativistic fluid modes in various configurations - scalar, vector, and tensor - and found the differences between their behavior in divergence-based and relaxation-time-approximation models. Our comparison also shows correspondence with first-order causal theories and highlights how a specific divergence-based model can predict damped tensor waves. This aligns with kinetic theory's results. It's interesting that both hydrodynamic and holographic fluids display similar properties. These findings reinforce the feasibility of using hydrodynamics to analyze the interaction between gravitational waves and fluids.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is insufficient, even after accounting for energy inflation from inflated regions. This deficiency is compounded by the limitations of the models, including constraints based on the parameters of inflation. As a result, the hypothesis remains unlikely, supporting the alternative explanation that the radiowave signals are generated by cosmic miniquasars formed following cosmic inflation.

Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processors with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to enable Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) at a secure computing offloading level, such as cloud computing. The VSP safeguards user codes within a Remote Semi-Honest (RSH) framework, protecting against malicious access attempts by the cloud while ensuring the execution of user-provided codes with potentially malicious inputs. Key innovations within VSP include a customized processor architecture and a customized IBM 8080 microprocessor emulator, both engineered to optimize performance and security through the employment of four low-level operations and four levels of Opcodes. To achieve this, the VSP integrates a 32 8-bit Wide Register with Standard Input/Output (I/O) interfaces, all encrypted with ABE-FHE abstractions. The paper details a cloud computing scenario in which a malicious cloud offloading executes user codes while keeping user data, codes, and inputs encrypted with ABE-FHE abstractions. The VSP then processes these instructions on a processed board with four levels of Opcodes, resulting in output data that is encrypted and accessible to both the user and the cloud with ABE-FHE abstractions. The VSP achieves this through the incorporation of four low-level operations: read memory, write memory, read I/O, and write I/O - all computed with FHE computations. To enable a realistic computing environment with real-world applications

Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is considered 'forbidden' in satisfiable instances.

A new PTAS is developed for general CSPs with constraints that have multiple values on certain graph classes, such as planar d-degrees graphs with a limited connectivity threshold.

The findings reduce the maximum CSP approximation scheme complexity for certain graph classes and narrow the complexity gap between maximum and minimum CSP values for specific constraint satisfaction problems.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance from self-attention weight matrices in pre-trained language models to evaluate sentence structures. Further experiments demonstrate the significance of linear projection matrices in self-attention for accurate parsing. Consequently, the unsupervised models were transformed into few-shot parsing models, FPOA and FPIO, to learn better parsing matrices with limited annotated trees. On the Penn Treebank dataset, the unsupervised model UPIO achieved parsing results on a par with current best techniques on short sentences, while the few-shot model FPIO offered superior performance over comparable models when trained with only eight correctly annotated dependencies.

High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated learning algorithms have not been extensively explored, particularly in complex urban settings. In this context, we develop an advanced semantic segmentation model, named HighResolution SEmantic Network for Hyperspectral Images (SERHYP). SERHYP is the first hyperspectral image segmentation framework to utilize concurrent spatial, spectral, and deep feature resolution refinement. It is further optimized to efficiently process high-resolution HSI images by leveraging on-demand multi-scale grouped convolutional operators and efficient in-place hyperspectral feature fusion. By refining multiple resolution streams within the feature extraction process, SERHYP is able to effectively extract rich multi-scale features that are then used to generate accurate high-resolution segmentation maps. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive dataset comprising 16,531 annotated pixels, referred to as the RSTU-GISBQHgHYP. Experimental evaluations on indoor and outdoor scenes demonstrate that SERHYP significantly outperforms leading low-resolution image segmentation models and exhibits robust generalization capabilities across diverse HSI datasets.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, we expect such stars to exhibit similar rotation rates across their entirety, but instead, we have observed a substantial difference in rotation speed between the core and the surface - a phenomenon known as differential rotation. The star in question is 71 Tauri, and our findings were derived from the analysis of its angular diameter following the direct imaging of its cross-section through the use of the Very Large Telescope's squinting technique. The measurement of its optical spectrum through the analysis of its zonal variations revealed a considerable variation in speed, with the equatorial regions spinning at 0.57 ± 0.10 km/s and the polar regions at 0.83 ± 0.15 km/s. The rate of spinning of 71 Tauri is notably lower than that of the sun. The measured size of its angular diameter was found to be 2.88 ± 0.18 miliseconds of arc. The size of its angular diameter varied from 2.72 to 2.99 miliseconds of arc. The size of its angular diameter was found not to be affected by varying distances. The size of its angular diameter varied from 2.72 to 2.99 miliseconds of arc. The size of its angular diameter was found not to be affected by varying distances.

In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model without a bound on the number of working memory registers. This has led some researchers to propose a more structured RAM model with a bounded number of memory units, but others have challenged this norm and argued for a more flexible computation model. This paper aims to address these debates by introducing a new class, known as LIN, which is comprised of algorithms requiring a linear number of memory steps and is robust against various modifications, including alterations in the computation model and the removal of input output operations. By identifying the LIN class as a fundamental component of algorithmic complexity theory, this paper demonstrates its significance and provides a solid foundation for future exploration in algorithmic complexity by showcasing the distinct computational complexities of two fundamental problems, the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) and the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem, with respect to the LIN class.

To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting session-based recommendation models that predict the next item users will choose, researchers combined self-supervised learning with co-training. They proposed an enhanced framework by leveraging a session-based graph to create informative, not artificially sparse, data for these models. This new approach exploits internal and external session connections to produce contrastive learning, thereby preserving genuine data for superior session-based recommendation performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the success of this innovative method in achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmark datasets.

This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation that maps group ring components to a unified element. We investigate the properties of this transformation and establish the conditions under which it yields LCD codes from group ring codings. We also discuss the maximum possible distance for these LCD codes, considering variables like the group ring size and length of the code. Our findings are further substantiated through the presentation of several concrete examples of LCD codes obtained via this construction method.

We examine period integrals of graph-related functions over edges, calculating canonical forms and determining resurgent properties of associated hypergeometric functions. These calculations apply to all graphs, allowing for an analysis of the six hypergeometric functions with the ability to generalize to any graph, regardless of its size. This analysis involves the evaluation of integrals and their relations to motivic functions, as well as their connections to Anderson-Bowden-Canakci graph-related functions and exceptional values in the solutions to a quadratic equation.

In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted an in-depth analysis of interacting one-dimensional systems and found that correlations greatly affect the topological structure, even altering the established classification in the absence of interactions. We developed a method using correlated hopping terms in the many-body Hamiltonian to incorporate correlations and derived the corresponding wavefunctions via the Bethe ansatz. Through this approach, we showed that correlations change the topological characteristics, leading to the emergence of new topological phases. We investigated and demonstrated this effect in the context of a fermionic system with a non-Hermitian hopping mechanism and found that correlations convert a Hermitian topological insulator into a non-Hermitian one. Our findings highlight the significance of correlations in shaping the topological structure of systems, thereby extending the established classification to include interacting non-Hermitian topological insulators.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to the SDMA case, enabling simultaneous data transmission from multiple antennas. A mathematical framework is developed to construct Golay complementary matrices in the case of multiple transmit antennas, utilizing ring cmddolay pairs and ring Golay pairs as building blocks. The proposed approach allows for the creation of Golay complementary matrices with an arbitrary number of columns, thereby accommodating general SDMA scenarios. Moreover, Golay ring complementary sequences, a specific type of Golay complementary matrix, are used to design Golay ring complementary matrices with an arbitrary number of columns, leveraging the existing lemmas and properties of ring Golay pairs.

Research on Higgs boson production is conducted, combining CMS data from 13 TeV LHC and previously collected data from 7 and 8 TeV LHC, totaling 104.6 fb^-1. The findings from four-lepton final state analysis provide joint constraints on Higgs boson width and its interaction with electroweak vector bosons. By applying matrix element techniques, production modes are separated and identified with excellent resolution. The results in intermediate and high-mass regions show consistency with standard model predictions. Assuming standard model-like couplings, the Higgs boson width is constrained between 0.4 and 5.4 GeV. The results in low-mass regions reveal slight excess in Higgs boson width with a 95% confidence level upper limit of 5.5 GeV.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, researchers address the complexities of analyzing numerous spectral bands within bi-temporal hyperspectral images. This study proposes a cutting-edge approach using a novel deep convolutional autoencoder that fuses features across hierarchical levels and receptive fields. By utilizing an unsupervised change detection technique, it overcomes the limitations of other label-dependent methods. By integrating various techniques to identify residual changes and construct a net effect, it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised change detection. Utilizing a hierarchical approach, it successfully resolves the partial distinctiveness problem in residual change detection. Furthermore, it overcomes the challenges posed by noise in hyperspectral images by utilizing a novel noise modeling technique, enabling more accurate change detection in noisy images. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method.

Consider the set $\mathcal{S}$ of squares and let $\mathcal{W}$ be a subset of natural numbers such that when you combine these two sets with addition, the result encompasses all natural numbers greater than or equal to some finite number $N_0$. Now, the $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ denotes the count of all possible pairs of $s$ from $\mathcal{S}$ and $w$ from $\mathcal{W}$ whose sum is equal to $n$. Previous studies by Ben Green and Tamar Zieve revealed that the function $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{W}}(n)$ grows additively at a rate that isn't linear. In this research, we refine their findings by providing evidence for a stronger statement - specifically that the difference between the sum of squares function and a linear growth function diverges to infinity with high probability, given certain conditions are met. To accomplish this, we leverage properties of diagonal flows associated with these sets, utilizing methods from ergodic theory and effectively computing spectral data for the corresponding algebraic variety.

Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that interacts with the wave functions of electrons, holes, and phonons. In silicon, this phenomenon is more pronounced due to confined particles in narrow regions. Phosphorus dopants can be used as quantum dots to study tunneling between adjacent orbitals and the exchange of particles. Researchers have developed an effective Hamiltonian to incorporate these processes and particle exchanges into a model. This model demonstrates a high level of accuracy in predicting energies and wave functions for various configurations. Future applications of this model include simulating complex many-body systems and their associated phenomena.

Several disciplines have been influenced by optimization techniques in various real-world scenarios, and as a result, there is an increasing need for efficient optimization tools. In order to meet this demand, the LibOPT project was initially introduced in a 2009 paper, and we are now publishing an updated update, highlighting key advancements made during the past five years. This updated report primarily focuses on cooperative and coevolutionary optimization techniques, as well as other future-related topics. Several new ideas have been incorporated to reflect the significant progress made in these areas. This updated report is an extension of the original 2009 paper, and it is intended to facilitate future research by highlighting the promising aspects of cooperative and coevolutionary optimization, as well as providing practical guidance on how to utilize LibOPT effectively.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive but not (m+1)-transitive, we say that Aut(X) has the m-transitivity property. This research investigates varieties with the transitivity property for nearly every m, and specifically focuses on the cases of m = 2 and m = 3. It involves finding the conditions under which the action of Aut(X) on the tangent space T_0X is m-transitive, and provides answers for specific types of varieties, such as those that are not of type 1 according to their type 1 classification, and certain types of unirational varieties. This research also explores connections between these conditions and problems related to the non-existence of sections for fibrations over projective space, and the existence of non-constant rational maps with a specific composition structure.

In non-commutative space-time deformations, the definition of identical particles breaks down. These models are described by non-abelian space symmetries represented by a four-momentum group. Our approach recognizes that for multi-particle states, the total system momentum is the only well-defined property. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition of individual particle momenta, which become ambiguous. Our results indicate that previous Fock space constructions were flawed due to incorrect momentum definitions and lack of implementation of additional anti-commutative symmetry constraints. We propose a revised Fock space framework that accurately represents quantum field theories in non-commutative space-time deformations. These Deformations are naturally occurring in certain models of non-commutative space-time and can be seen as a non-linear effect of non-commutative deformation of the Poincaré group. Our work lays the foundation for a detailed study of quantum field theory in this specific non-commutative scenario.

A advanced technique for studying wide bandgap semiconductors is presented, allowing for a precise measurement of charge transport properties at a highly detailed spatial level. This is achieved through the integration of a wide bandgap semiconductor substrate within a MeV ion beam-induced micro-patterned veil technique. As a result, a significant charge density is generated near the ion trajectory with localized spatial distribution. This technique has been successfully applied to study charge transport in CVD-grown CVD C crystals, measuring the electric field along the crystal's axis with sub-millimeter resolution.

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models, incorporating Set Ensembles, Multi-task learning, and Transformer-based architectures, using diverse features. Our approach successfully identified misogynistic content in two challenging dataset categories. Our results indicate that our models achieved top-tier marks in both task types, securing first and second place overall rankings.

This study centres around the solvability of a distinct class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations that take into account past influences within their generators, under Lipschitz condition it's demonstrated that the existence and uniqueness of such equations are assured. Furthermore, a key comparison theorem has been formulated.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation.

Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, whereas distributed computation explores the balance between computation and communication within a distributed system. This paper delves into the connection between caching and computation by addressing a fundamental question: can caching methods be adapted for computation tasks? The authors investigate a scenario in which a distributed computing system with multiple devices generates and processes data at remote locations. To reduce data transfer between devices, the model incorporates data caching at all devices and includes a network capacity constraint. A specific caching scheme is proposed, which distributes a global file equally among all devices and computes it locally. It is proven that this scheme achieves optimal results in terms of reduced data transfer when there are only two devices involved. However, the model's complexity increases exponentially as the number of devices increase in scenarios where all devices contribute equally to the computation. An alternative caching scheme is proposed, which distributes a global file evenly but allows each device to choose its contribution to the computation. The model shows that this scheme leads to global optimality in terms of reduced data transfer when there are no constraints on the devices' contribution and results in minimal transfer in scenarios where all devices contribute equally. Finally, the model is applied to a scenario with a binary addition computation task and interesting properties are observed.

We establish a formalization of the Scott model in univalent type theory, adopting a constructive and predicative framework. To capture the essence of non-terminating processes in PCF, we employ the lifting monad from topos theory, which has been adapted for univalent type theory by Escard\'o and Knapp. Our work confirms that using the lifting monad provides a viable way to handle partiality within univalent type theory, and we also demonstrate that a predicative and constructive Scott model is achievable. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality.

This brief note manually calculates the degrees of certain Eisenstein series associated with the symplectic group Sp_4, confirming earlier computer-generated results obtained by Chan-Chai. By applying the formula for Eisenstein series involving characters of minimal and next-to-minimal type, specifically in the context of Sp_4, we determine the degrees of these Eisenstein series and relate them to representation degrees of type 10 and 20, combining this with local factors to obtain our result.

Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that enables a mobile robotic arm to safely move through a cluttered environment while avoiding obstacles and maintaining a stable walking gait.
A control framework is devised to balance these competing demands, with a novel form of constraint propagation used to efficiently address a complex problem.
A key feature of the proposed method is its ability to adapt to varying gaits without necessitating reconfiguration.
Simulation results validate the efficacy of the proposed method in a range of scenarios.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Researchers have suggested the application of quantum interferometry in gravitational physics for precise measurements of small masses. However, current theories based on linear quantum mechanics may not fully apply to the behavior of particles under extreme conditions, leading to potential losses in measurement accuracy. To address this limitation, a new approach known as nonlinear quantum mechanics is being developed, although it lacks a solid theoretical foundation. So far, nonlinear effects have only been observed in limited situations and the search for a solid theoretical framework is ongoing. One possibility is that the description of particle interactions changes based on the reference frame used, but this would require a new quantum mechanics. Interestingly, there are similarities between this idea and the principles of nonlinear quantum mechanics. If the particle behaves differently based on the reference frame, then the particle's properties may be linked to the observer, leading to a possible connection between the particle's properties and the observer's reference frame. This raises further questions and opens up new avenues for research, including the possibility of observing nonlinear effects in experiments and developing new applications in quantum information processing and interferometry.

This paper aims to accomplish two distinct objectives. Firstly, it seeks to establish a unicity theorem for meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, under the constraint of limited intersection with hypersurfaces. Secondly, the paper aims to prove a unicity theorem for the case of nondegenerate meromorphic mappings that share a specified number of hyperplanes in a particular geometric configuration.

Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises points where the codimension of the solution set matches the number of equations in the system. Historically, the nondegenerate locus has been obtained using ideal-theoretic techniques like saturation ideals and equidimensional decompositions. We propose an algorithm leveraging signature-based features of Gröbner basis algorithms to directly calculate the nondegenerate locus in a Gröbner basis-based setting. This method integrates seamlessly with existing Gröbner basis solvers by incorporating signature-based conditions as termination criteria. We demonstrate the efficacy of this new method through computational experiments.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central Au+Au collisions at Keck Laboratory's PHENIX detector, which operates at a 200 GeV energy at RHIC. These collisions have been compared to both p+p and $A$+$B$ interactions at intermediate and low $p_T$ levels, revealing a notable increase in photon production relative to expected values in Au+Au collisions, especially at lower transverse momentum ranges. Notably, this increase is more pronounced when Au+Au collisions are contrasted with binary-collision scaled Au+Au or $d$+$A$ interactions. These findings suggest a growing photon production as the collision environment becomes more complex, which is in line with an increasing trend observed in smaller-sized heavy-ion experiments at lower beam energies.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We develop a new method for determining hypergraph extremality and apply it to calculate the asymptotic extremal function of the tetrahedron graph under our novel framework. The codegree squared sum, or '2g(U)', of an n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph G or its epigraph graph E(G) represents the sum of squares of codegree between every pair of vertices in G or E(G). We identify an upper bound for the codegree squared sum '2g(Kn^3(U))' of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 or its epigraph graph E(K4^3) over all K4^3-free 3-uniform n-vertex hypergraphs. The known Erdos-Sos conjecture proposed that the codegree squared sum '2g(Kn^3(U))' equals 4n-4. Our work presents an alternative viewpoint on the problem by decomposing hypergraphs based on the epigraph graph property and representing a K4^3-free hypergraph's codegree vector components as those of a K4^3-free epigraph graph. The new approach leads to an algorithm that generates all possible components of a K4^3-free

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. The proposed technique not only ensures a smooth visual experience but also significantly boosts rendering speed by reducing the number of alpha tests. Comparative tests using various rendering libraries further validate the algorithm's efficiency.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values at specified points. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance between points. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and local smoothing properties. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

Pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe) are a crucial source of high-energy cosmic rays, illuminating the Galaxy's magnetic field and particle propagation. Studying PWNe's gamma-ray emission helps differentiate between cosmic-ray injection and escape rates. This, in turn, informs models of cosmic-ray propagation and the Galaxy's magnetic field properties. We have conducted a comprehensive search for PWNe using the Large Area Telescope on the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, covering 10 years from 2008 to 2017. With a significant sensitivity improvement compared to previous surveys, our research has triggered over 200 new sources and provided more than 240 significant detections of known PWNe. This extensive dataset allows for detailed analysis of PWNe's characteristics and will likely lead to groundbreaking findings in understanding cosmic-ray propagation and the Galaxy's magnetic field properties.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and incorporate features derived from shallow networks and image processing techniques to enhance dataset utility.
We then devise a novel fusion system to integrate low-level visual cues and temporal context, and present comprehensive experimental results for comparison with 13 prominent models.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have explored the use of data-driven control methods. However, current controllers either rely on extensive data collection for every possible scenario or require the solution of an under-determined algebraic equation, using the infinite-dimensionality of the system, often resulting in poor generalization or unrealistically time-consuming calculations. In light of these challenges, we propose an new control method that leverages the use of Dynamic Mode Decomposition to reduce the system to a controllable dynamical system, making it possible to apply optimal control techniques. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by successfully grasping multiple objects, including various sizes and shapes, using a controllable actuator and a simple flat surface gripper attached to a robotic finger.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods.

A mysterious source, 3C 279, has generated significant interest due to its properties of high variability and polarized radiation across various wavelengths. A potential explanation for these properties is the presence of a jet-emitting electron beam. Researchers have observed the source characteristics, aiming to form a comprehensive picture of the source structure. A new, insightful approach to analyze variability properties is the Rydberg recombination line monitoring method, providing distinct empty cone and filled cone patterns for different spectral indices. Assuming the source follows a shell pattern, specific Rydberg recombination line monitoring patterns can only be achieved if the source has a significant dip in 25-30 degrees. Other phenomena, such as photoionization of nearby clouds or synchrotron radiation of nearby filaments, can also produce observable Rydberg recombination line monitoring patterns together with variability patterns, but these require a more intricate configuration. A potential challenge in confirming the variable patterns is the source complexity and limited sampling points. If the source has a significant dip in 25-30 degrees, empty cone and filled cone patterns for different spectral indices can be observed during certain states, and variability patterns can be observed during other states producing empty and filled cone patterns. A young compact symmetric object, characterized by a steep spectrum, may be identified through further observation.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in predicting survival times, as evidenced by comprehensive experiments using real-world data from 422 patients with non-small cell lung cancer.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated aerosol radiative transfer models and simulations of radiative transfer, synthetic spectra corresponding to various WLSZK density perturbations are generated. These simulated spectra are then utilized to train a deep learning model, enabling the prediction of density perturbations from observed spectra. Multiple radiative transfer models are employed to remove biases, and cross-validation is performed to validate the results. The performance of this deep learning model is evaluated using Maiden's likelihood analysis and compared with a Bayesian analysis on ZLSWK data.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated a substantial Twitter dataset with 1,920
entries, aiming to develop a sophisticated model capable of accurately extracting sentiment
from unstructured tweets while disregarding noise from irrelevant posts. We employed
various neural network techniques, such as transfer learning with BERT, and explored the use
of transfer learning with convolutional neural networks to build our analysis. Following
evaluation, we identified and analyzed our models' mistakes to develop and refine our
analysis. Ultimately, we were able to engineer our models to achieve impressive accuracy
rates of 0.742 and 0.734 in leave-one-out and k-fold cross-validation, respectively, on
classification, and demonstrated the potential for further enhancement.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human interaction data, making it
incompatible with growing AI models like GPT-3. To address this issue, we propose
a new approach using weak supervision with multi-task training, combining
conversational tasks like persona preservation and safety constraints. We have
designed a novel, weakly-supervised training method that employs auxiliary tasks
to enhance conversation coherence and realism, utilizing natural language
inconsistency and conversational breaches as positive labels. Furthermore, we
assert the importance of incorporating a persona feature in open-domain dialogue
systems and must not be omitted during training. We have also developed a new
metric to evaluate dialog safety, which we utilize to guide dialog completion.
Experimental results have demonstrated the efficacy of our proposed method in
maintaining persona consistency and enhancing dialog safety while producing more
natural and engaging outputs.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Failing to accurately account for SGWMB could lead to incorrect conclusions, but properly investigating it might enable the detection of supermassive binary black holes. Furthermore, studying SGWMB offers a novel method to identify gravitational wave memory and provides an opportunity to advance our understanding of gravity theory.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; this framework predicts the universe underwent a phase transition around the time of the universe's birth that may create ripples still detectable today. If this phase transition happened under the right conditions, it could have led to the creation of cosmic strings with properties similar to gravitational waves; these strings might be detectable by future instruments including a planned telescope that will search for these ripples. The temperature at which these ripples are most effective is similar to the temperature at which certain properties of certain materials change, and this phase transition temperature could be lowered if a certain type of field behaves in a certain way.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge involves using language that is easily understood and is not confined to specific technical expertise. This abstract presents a core model for a language that can evolve and is used in various contexts, with a focus on its application to semantic communication systems. It discusses the benefits of and necessity for language development and presents a framework that enables its construction and adaptation across multiple domains. Furthermore, we highlight the potential for and advantages of using language that is rooted in everyday, natural language to facilitate effective communication.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, yet it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. While these models can be computationally demanding, hindering their feasibility in certain scenarios, continuous advancements in technology and mathematical modeling enable the development of faster, more accurate systems. A hybrid word suggestion model proposed here, combining elements of Naive Bayes and latent semantic analysis and considering context provided by surrounding words in the sentence, demonstrates considerable promise. Notably, this model achieved a 44.2% accuracy rating in the MSR Sentence Completion Challenge.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention-based mechanism and demonstrates its effectiveness on currently top-performing deep learning models for session-based recommendation, including STAMP and NARM.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis or antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic behavior similar to that of a single active particle, while others exhibit a longer persistence time and increased chemotactic response. By contrast, dimers in other configurations display antichemotactic behavior and may maintain a fixed position with respect to activity gradients. The dimer's ability to navigate activity gradients can be enhanced through interaction parameters that influence its movement.

A comprehensive simulation of fractured porous media flow requires an in-depth understanding of the fracture system and precise calculation of Fracture Permeability Tensor. The current DFM approach transforms this task into two major challenges: Fracture Description and Fracture Matrix Permeability Calculation. Although DFM facilitates flexible fracture descriptions, it can result in excessively large systems of equations. We develop a new 'Weakly Coupled Multiscale' approach to address these challenges by leveraging pre-computed Fracture Interaction Data to determine the Fracture Matrix Permeability Tensor, thus combining Multiple fractures' influence on the adjacent grid block's permeability tensor. This approach is now coupled with a novel Multiscale Coarse Grid Source Term, allowing the transfer of information between the small-scale fractures and the coarse-scale grid. We pre-compute the Fracture Interaction Data using Local Fractional Flow Simulations, which are then used to determine the Fracture Matrix Permeability Tensor. This approach is shown to significantly outperform the standard Single fracture description in DFM simulations, while also reducing the cost associated with Local Fractional Flow Simulations.

This research focuses on developing an autonomous collision avoidance system for large drone swarms. A key approach in achieving this goal is the concept of negotiation, which typically relies on communication between lead aircraft to resolve potential conflicts. However, this method has limitations, such as increased communication requirements and potential bottlenecks. This paper explores an alternative strategy that eliminates the need for communication by using local interactions and swarm intelligence, which is demonstrated through a test case involving a large number of unmanned aerial vehicles operating in a dense environment and effectively avoiding each other.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that -1 and 0 are unique eigenvalues, while 1 has the highest possible multiplicity all over the graph. Furthermore, the study derives the minimum number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to these eigenvalues. Additionally, it derives the maximum and minimum eigenvalue bounds for the Seidel matrix of a chain graph and identifies its eigenvectors for certain eigenvalues.

In the context of semi-martingale decomposition, fractional Brownian motion (fBm) stands out due to its unique combination of non-Markovian properties and the absence of a natural filtration framework. This fBm representation theorem addresses this issue by providing a canonical representation that suits the needs of model builders. The representation involves the sum of a continuous process with absolutely continuous integral, a compensated Poisson process, and an independent fBm. This framework is particularly useful for the modeling of physical systems, as it is often challenging to define a suitable filtration for such systems. The application of this representation can be seen in the modeling of a system that involves interaction between the Inland Waterways network and the Charente river in France, as mandated by the European Union's Directive on Directive 2003/51/EC.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've derived key mathematical expressions, including the periodic Dirac operator's norm and geometric multiplicity within the space of $\mathcal{H}^1$, and we've identified the essential spectrum and some real eigenvalues, alongside a relevant Hilbert space eigenfunction pattern.

As traffic congestion in metropolitan areas continues to grow, it often causes congestion on local roads and high demand for local data services. Traditional methods using base stations may not suffice to meet these localized needs and also result in expensive data plans for users. To address this, this study proposes an innovative solution where vehicles in traffic act as temporary relays to enhance network capacity, particularly for users in congested areas. By leveraging vehicle positioning and traffic information, the suggested solution dynamically establishes and adjusts cooperative routes to maximize network performance, focusing on minimizing delay for users in high-traffic areas. Notably, the algorithm's effectiveness has been confirmed through successful simulations in multiple scenarios, including various road conditions and numbers of vehicles.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established assessment process. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we need labeled data, but existing work relies on automatic tags, which are not always accurate or reliable, creating issues. Instead of addressing these problems separately, we developed a self-improving system that combines data curation and machine learning in a continuous cycle. It starts with a limited set of high-quality articles to train a model, which in turn helps readers to identify poor quality articles that require improvement. These articles are then edited by Wikipedia editors who label them as candidates for improvement, feeding the model with new data. This process repeats indefinitely, and our results show significant progress in detecting articles for improvement, surpassing performance achieved through solely human efforts.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to the network's decision is quantified by its contrastive divergence, which serves as a proxy for transferability. This information is used to prioritize samples in adversarial training, making the process more efficient by reducing the need for multiple iterations and potential errors. Moreover, when access to the original data isn't possible, a new criterion called relative entropy is proposed to rank samples for counterfactual evaluation, which in turn helps improve the model's fairness by prioritizing samples with high relative fairness scores for training. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of these methods.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is further explored. We establish that non-abelian solvmanifolds can be covered by almost abelian solvmanifolds, suitable for T-dualisable $C^*$-algebras. In addition, we identify the duals of torus bundles as examples of T-dualisable $C^*$-algebras arising from almost abelian solvmanifolds.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Through thorough evaluations on multiple complex environments, CoIL has been shown to accelerate learning, boost performance, and extend learning durability to even higher levels.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance for polar codes in channels with arbitrary noise, and demonstrates the function's applicability to polarization-adjusted convolutional codes, which can bypass the convolutional code termination issue. The PAC code's error-correction performance is enhanced using the proposed metric, resulting in reduced decoding latency without compromising its convolutional-like characteristics and minimum distance properties. Moreover, the PAC code's latency is directly proportional to the channel noise level, making it a noise-rate-constrained latency optimizer.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to normalize hand movements and simplify the complexity of hand geometry. The proposed HandTrackNet consists of a feature extraction module that extracts key features from the initial representation, a canonicalization module to standardize hand joint positions, a deformation module that predicts the shape and movement of hand joints, and a refinement module that refines the estimates through temporal self-correction. To evaluate the effectiveness of HandTrackNet, we created a large and diverse dataset called HO3D-Sup-Perm, by further expanding the original HO3D dataset. Experimental results show that the proposed HandTrackNet outperforms alternative methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, and significantly reduces the complexity of hand joint geometry. The proposed method and dataset are now available online for further research and testing at the address: https://github.com/ncllab/nclimu-HandTrackNet.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods.

Calculations involving novel dark matter states within neutron stars have been explored through a network-inspired approach, combining equations of state, dark matter properties, and processes such as neutrino emission through dark matter interactions or beta decay. The primary dark matter destruction reactions within neutron stars are found to be $ ar{\chi}\chiightarrow
u ar{
u}$ and $ ar{\chi}N\gamma
u$. These reactions significantly impact the ejection of dark matter from neutron stars, with the presence of dark matter interactions with ordinary particles leading to the emergence of a characteristic "bump" in the resulting neutrino spectra. The shape and intensity of this "neutrino burst" significantly varies based on the dark matter properties and neutron star composition, with the intensity reaching neutrino flux levels of $10^{8-12}$cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, contingent upon a range of dark matter properties. The detection of such a "neutrino burst" by KM3NeT or other neutrino telescopes could provide a unique opportunity to investigate novel dark matter states.

The ongoing UNIONS project is the most recent comprehensive optical survey to date, focusing on Sloan's g, r, and i band imaging data from the 4th Sloan Digital Sky Survey release. This paper reports on the completion of the UNIONS project's initial data release, comprising 845,167 galaxies with shear-measured biases. Conducted across approximately 0.95 steradians of sky, the project's weak-lensing maps were created using a high-precision shear tomography algorithm, achieving a 1% uncertainty. By applying the NFW model, the project estimated its first weak-lensing cosmological results, yielding a universe in which the dark energy density is approximately 0.69 GeV/cm^3 and the matter density is 0.31 GeV/cm^3, with a matter fluctuation amplitude of 0.03 and neutrino effective mass of 0.29 eV. The project's approach to correctly interpreting the E-G lensing bias allows it to accurately model both the project's systematic and statistical uncertainties. With a planned expansion to 1.6 steradians of sky in the upcoming 5th SDSS release, the project is prepared to provide higher-precision weak-lensing results in future publications.

A notable result from Hermann, Sarig, and Quas demonstrates that for any irrational $\alpha$ with both $\alpha$ and $1-\alpha$ being non-zero, the parity of the cardinalities of sets $E([0,1],\alpha,p)$ and $E([0,1],\alpha,q)$ is evenly distributed as $p$ and $q$ vary over all natural numbers, where $E([0,1],\alpha,p)$ and $E([0,1],\alpha,q)$ denote respectively the sets of points $x$ in the interval $[0,1]$ for which either $x+\alpha BP\{x\}$ is an integer divisible by $p$, and $x+\alpha BQ\{x\}$ is an integer divisible by $q$. In this study, we derive a consequence which allows us to determine the parity of the difference in the cardinalities of $E([0,1],\alpha,p)$ and $E([0,1],\alpha,q)$ for any irrational $\alpha$ and natural numbers $p$ and $q$.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes three-dimensional correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally determined parameters are employed to determine the critical temperatures associated with BKT transitions as well as long-range order. Finite-size scaling of the spin stiffness based on these data shows a perfect agreement with the theory regarding scaling behavior across different dimensions.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a qubit to the Standard Model makes it a more complex theoretical framework, referred to as the aqMSM. This enhanced model is highly capable of explaining dark matter and matter-antimatter asymmetry. The focus of our research is the type of dark matter that can be formed during symmetry breaking and when neutrinos acquire mass. The study finds that the model's dark matter is composed of a mixture of aqMSMinos and weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs), with the proportion depending on the specific values of various physical constants. The paper includes a detailed mathematical model that describes how the masses of the model's various particles form and evolve over time.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating $n$-qubit circuit simulations with $\epsilon$ precision, achieving an runtime of $O(\mathrm{poly}(n,m)/\epsilon^2)$, and also leads to enhanced bounds for simulating specific quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates, which normally require an exponential number of classical gates.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by comparing our results with the standard quintessence 
model. We examine two situations: a non-relativistic and a radiation-dominated era.
We will highlight differences between TDRE and standard quintessence by looking at 
field values, their evolution, and energy density distributions. Finally, we will 
investigate implications on the age of the universe.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To ensure high-quality spectra, we conducted various processing steps such as removing nighttime stars, detecting and removing spectra with obvious anomalies, inducing signal suppression, and rejecting low signal-to-noise ratio spectra. After these operations, the total number of spectra lower than 10k was around 734,000 for low-resolution and 234,000 for medium-resolution. All data have been made accessible on the LAMOST website.

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To enhance throughput, the approach involves utilizing multiple SRAM banks in parallel. Furthermore, by applying a statistical method to characterize random number generation, the TRNG's statistical quality is evaluated without the need for external, specialized hardware, thereby reducing implementation complexity. In addition, by analyzing and optimizing the SRAM's inherent timing irregularities at a detailed level using a simulation tool, the proposed TRNG's randomness extraction mechanism is optimized to maximize entropy extraction while minimizing unnecessary data samples. A prototype based on this design has demonstrated its efficacy through experimental testing with an SoC containing four SRAM banks, each featuring 16 KB of storage. This has yielded an average throughput of 2.44 Mbps, 15.88 pJ/bit energy efficiency, latency of 1.96 ns, and high-quality random numbers with bits not predictable.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process information as single binary units and produce notable current fluctuations to distinguish between the device's off and on states. Furthermore, simulations exposed the potential for self-organization and self-assembly into solid films that could be used to produce low-cost, high-capacity storage devices.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality at the level of the underlying Feynman integrals, the process of computing amplitudes becomes simplified. This approach is characterized by a direct relation between loop variables and external particles, making it particularly suitable for numerical evaluations. In this context, the authors investigate various aspects of loop variables and their relationships with external particles, exploring constraints on these variables in the context of loop-tree duality. They also examine the influence of crossing symmetries on this duality, demonstrating how different crossodings can be implemented while preserving the loop-tree duality framework. To validate their findings, the authors provide numerical results for two-loop amplitudes in various configurations, such as Higgs+jet production and the decay of a Z boson into fermions.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing us to express a particular operator on two-dimensional square lattices as a direct sum of non-Hermitian block-tridiagonal operators.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the impact of $q$-deformation on a model optomechanical system, specifically its ability to support spontaneous optical transitions. By examining the resulting Hamiltonian, it becomes evident that $q$-deformation gives rise to novel mechanisms through the creation of new, $q$-dependent photonic states. As a result, it is possible to investigate how $q$-deformation affects thermal equilibrium states. This research demonstrates that $q$-deformation can alter first-order phase transitions, either suppressing them or causing them to vanish entirely, depending on the value of $q$. By exploring various scenarios, it becomes clear that $q$-deformation is capable of converting second-order phase transitions into either first-order or continuous processes. Ultimately, this study suggests that $q$-deformation is a valuable tool for optimizing photonic properties and improving our understanding of phase transitions in optomechanical systems.

In a previous study, I developed a model where two identical rotors were positioned parallel to each other and I examined the dynamics of this system against a black hole background that resembles Minkowski space yet for a limited radius is significantly different. The Two-Rotors Model appears to be an effective simplification for understanding the dynamics of composite systems consisting of multiple objects such as scatters, or more complexly, connected closed loops. This document focuses on deriving the equations of motion for a specific type of negative scissors state consisting of two clasically linked bodies where the counter-rotating scatters maintain a fixed distance. It also discusses how these entities move through a background that is both curved and static.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. We identified unique electron correlations and structural distortions in this thin film oxides, contributing to the observed insulating state. Our research suggests that ultra-thin transition-metal oxides require specific treatments to maintain their bulk properties.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread phenomenon has been explored through numerous experiments and related theories. In this research, we examine anisotropic diffusion by simulating a random walking particle that moves in a two-dimensional space with different diffusion rates in horizontal and vertical directions. Findings show that such a system can exhibit the Saffman-Duke anomalous diffusion behavior under specific conditions, and by comparing our simulation results with existing theoretical predictions, we validate the proposed distribution formula for understanding anomalous diffusion in complex systems.
