This study investigates the impact of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis reveals that cryptocurrency markets exhibit both weak and robust patterns of dependence. The US dollar-denominated cryptocurrency network displays a mixture of positive and negative Granger causality, implying that some cryptocurrencies' log returns can predict others, while others' log returns cannot predict each other. The logarithmic returns of cryptocurrency trading volumes in major networks are linked to the distributed ledger technology of cryptocurrency XBP, whereas in smaller networks, XBP's log returns are causal to the distributed ledger technology of cryptocurrency XEM. Furthermore, the US dollar-denominated cryptocurrency network shows a weekly cycle similar to weekly oscillations in many other markets. The majority of cryptocurrencies' log returns are uncorrelated, yet many show a negative correlation with their own past, indicating volatility oscillations. The stable coins dominate high-order statistical dependencies, while showing weak or no dependence with other major price factors in the network.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds, which in turn reflect sunlight and impact Earth's energy balance by influencing albedo. Understanding the various pathways of particle formation is essential to quantifying this process. Researchers have outlined several mechanisms of particle formation and analyzed their applicability in different environments, highlighting the need for further research in this area.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a cover over their codomain, resulting in new compact perception pairs that compactify their original counterparts, which possess totally bounded datasets. Moreover, we present compatibility conditions for these embeddings and demonstrate that they're satisfied by our constructions.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in fluids. In a study on this phenomenon, known as the Soret effect, researchers found that certain components of a binary mixture exhibited an unusual Soret coefficient when subjected to temperature gradients in an anisotropic solid structure. The calculations revealed that this phenomenon is not unique to certain materials and can occur in a wide range of materials with non-isotropic properties. The predictions have been confirmed by theoretical models, showing that certain properties of a material can enhance the Soret effect, while others can suppress it. The findings open up new avenues for researching and applying the Soret effect in materials with unique properties.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and it is often beneficial for these models to be interpretable and understandable. While simplicity is a highly valuable property, it is not well-defined in the context of deep learning models. This lack of definition prevents researchers from effectively evaluating the simplicity of deep models and implementing regularization techniques to control model complexity. This paper redefines simplicity in terms of geometric properties and demonstrates how certain deep neural network architectures can be viewed as 3D shapes. By applying this definition, we develop a method to measure the complexity of deep models and use this metric to investigate the effects of training parameters on model complexity. This study further explores how to utilize this new understanding of model complexity to regulate deep learning models and improve their performance.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model across diverse topics.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set distributions. We also investigate numerical methods for parameter estimation in detailed models, providing a framework that generalizes the approach of graphoid abstraction.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. This strategy corresponds with various empirical measures of social mobility. Moreover, we observe a paradox where, to promote long-term social mobility, it's often necessary to limit opportunities for individuals who have a higher socioeconomical standing. This challenge needs to be balanced against the benefits of providing such individuals with opportunities to utilize their existing socioeconomical advantages.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake (DPoS), resulting in Delegated RingCT (DeRCT). To enable fair voting rights among full nodes, DeRCT incorporates a customized voting mechanism tied to the Token Curated Research (TCR) platform. By extending DeRCT with a proof-of-stake consensus algorithm, we establish a robust foundation for scalable and transparent decentralized applications.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers at the CMS experiment in relation to LLR have examined proton-proton collisions occurring at a high energy level of 13 TeV.  The researchers have identified a significant relationship between real and imaginary parts of a particular theoretical prediction for processes involving multiple boson interactions.  Additionally, a search for rare events involving three massive bosons was conducted, and the results were compared to standard models.  The data analyzed came from approximately 35.9 billion proton collisions.  The researchers have also determined cross-section estimates for these multiple boson interactions.  More data is expected to potentially reveal hidden patterns among the data and the predicted standards.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations and validates the results using multiple evaluation methods. Additionally, the authors demonstrate the benefits of utilizing this new corpus for enhancing both HeBRT and HeTrebank.

We maintain fixed $p \in [1,\infty)$ and $K \in (0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\mu$. It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the dimension $d$ is less than or equal to $\frac{32e^2 (2K)^{2p}\log n}{\varepsilon^2}$, and for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, the inequality $||x_i - x_j||_p \leq ||y_i - y_j||_p \leq ||x_i - x_j||_p + \varepsilon$ always holds. Additionally, it is shown that the ball containing $y_1,\ldots,y_n$ has an approximate diameter relative to $\ell_p^d$ that is at least $\frac{\sqrt{\ln n}}{2}\max_{1\leq i\le n}||x_i||_p$, and that the introduced method can be utilized to solve the all-pairs shortest path problem in graphs, providing an algorithm with

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, challenges persist in machine learning, such as catastrophic forgetting, where continuous training causes trained models to forget previous skills after learning new ones. This reminds us of the issues Kenneth Cooper encountered when introducing 'catastrophic thinking' in the 1950s, describing how small changes in children's minds can significantly impact learning. If a significant change occurs, it becomes difficult for them to return to their previous state of mind. This analogy inspired the concept of cognitive restructurings, supporting the development of cooperative learning structures to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and promote continued learning in mechanics.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that significantly decreases computational demands, resulting in a nearly real-time capable safety filter design. The safety-guaranteeing capabilities of these advanced methods are illustrated through simulations involving a robotic arm navigating around obstacles.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as single photons switches, indistinguishable sources, and linear measurements, which can effortlessly bypass the standard free-space QKD system's security. Specifically, our proposed attack involves a collection stage where the quantum signal is intercepted and a photon source is activated to create numerous identical photons, each corresponding to a different receiver channel. Following this stage, the photons are split and directed to both receivers, where each is subjected to measurement by a secondary device. The secondary device then gathers data from the measurements and transmits it to the attacker, enabling them to access the actual key exchanged between the two main receivers. As a result, the attacker's side channel information exceeds the quantum bound, severely compromising the system's security.

Recent investigations into in-context learning with pre-trained language models have revealed that the performance of such models depends on various factors, including the source of pretraining data and instruction design. While there's significant interest in in-context learning, its limitations are often overlooked in favor of fine-tuning methods. Our aim is to expand the range of tasks where in-context learning is evaluated, and to examine its performance on three different datasets: a semantic parsing task, a natural language inference task, and a question-answering task. Our results indicate that in-context learning with large language models can achieve impressive performance on these tasks, and may potentially replace fine-tuning in various scenarios. Our findings also point out the need for further research on how to effectively craft instructional prompts.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the surrounding hot intracluster medium before ultimately fragmenting and creating numerous smaller clumps. These fragments act as nuclei, fostering further condensation through processes including Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, thereby nearly doubling the cold gas within a 75 million-year period. Cloud expansion appears to be determined by factors such as density and localized heat-producing mechanisms that either cause the cold gas to dissipate or cause it to shrink. Nevertheless, it is evident that galaxy clusters harbor substantial, kiloparsec cold gas, and this could provide sufficient material for the formation of dwarf galaxies within a billion years. This theoretical framework is supported by observations of the galaxy cluster Sersic 1204-51-1, which displays similar characteristics in the form of kiloparsec cold gas and numerous stellar fragments.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The
presentation includes precise measurements of observables connected to the
unitary triangles stemming from unitarity constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-
Maskawa matrix describing quark mixing, alongside recent $C\!P$ violation
measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons. Specific emphasis is given to an
analysis that initially identified $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and used
this effect to further refine constraints on the universal weak magnetic
momentum of quarks.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. These powerful new tools can be used to enhance string predictions at high-energy particle colliders like the LHC.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech stream is segmented into CVCs using an HMM-GMM framework, and then CVCs are segmented into basic units through a clustering technique based on their spectral features. The basic units in the C12 speech corpus, derived from British English, exhibit unique characteristics and are sufficient for test-time synthesis. The proposed units exhibit natural speech-like properties and are used for non-autonomous inference, enabling the transformation of speech into desired identities in the GAN-based voice conversion system SAGAN.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging optimization issue, resulting in computationally expensive solutions. To tackle this problem, we've developed a two-phase motion planning method for robots with multiple limbs, ensuring they maintain a stable posture while meeting force requirements. Our approach involves initial calculations to determine a starting point, followed by a series of local optimizations to refine the results, all within a predetermined time limit. To speed up the planning process, we've also introduced an octree data structure to accelerate search operations and reduce the computational burden. Our method effectively plans complex multi-limbed robots' movements within a limited time frame, even when subjected to external forces and constraints. Experimental results show that this method outperforms alternative methods, demonstrating a significant improvement in efficiency without compromising accuracy.

We introduce a fundamental requirement for achieving a physical transformation from one quantum state to another using a specific resource - a maximally coherent qubit state in this context - in affine quantum resource theories. This requirement is expressed as a singular value constraint and is applicable to any resource theory based on linear combinations of multiple copies of a single quantum state. Importantly, this condition surpasses existing regulations in certain resource theories, notably the quantum entanglement theory within bipartite settings. Furthermore, we present a method to determine if a particular quantum channel can be implemented without employing the resource, and we illustrate the practical implications of this concept through quantum entanglement examples.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the minimax problem, we frame it as a tight approximation of the original issue, enabling us to leverage the existing knowledge in robust optimization. Utilizing the Taylor expansion around a centralized reference point, we establish lower and upper bounds on the regularized total variance. These bounds enable us to create a tight approximation and subsequently, an efficient algorithm, DR-DSGD, which outperforms its conventional counterpart, DSGD. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in achieving lower communication overhead while tightly controlling regularization's influence on total variance.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations that incorporate magnetohydrodynamics and radiative transfer, researchers studied how protostellar jets form and behave in star-forming clouds under various initial conditions. They observed the formation of powerful outflows capable of emitting far ultraviolet radiation, a process that typically begins about 0.1 to 0.2 parsecs from the star. These outflows can only be explained by the presence of a strong magnetic field that allows material to be accelerated and ejected in high-velocity jets. The velocity and temperature of these jets match real-world observations of such phenomena. The mass of the star determines which processes will dominate the development of the outflow, with slower speeds associated with higher masses. The strength of the magnetic field also plays a crucial role, as very weak fields prevent the formation of the outflows, while extremely strong fields result in faster speeds but ultimately fail to eject material. The presence of a strong magnetic field allows material to be ejected in high-velocity jets. The strength of the magnetic field affects the formation of the outflows, with a certain threshold required to replicate real-world observations of such phenomena.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error, which collectively signify a system's risk level. This framework enables the optimization of safety standards (reduced in safe scenarios, increased in risky scenarios) to expand the system's performance capability, ultimately mitigating the risk posed by destabilizing factors. In the case of a second-order system subject to parameter-related uncertainties and disturbance forces, numerical simulations are conducted to verify the effectiveness of this strategy, with a local minimum safely optimizing the system's performance and not its risks, whereas a global minimum safely optimizes the system's performance and protects it against parameter-related risks.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect objects orbiting the Earth, which is increasingly recognized as a vital area of study. Focusing specifically on the influence of the Moon's gravitational force, we aimed to explore its impact on objects following specific trajectories. These objects would need to have properties similar to those of meteoric bodies, exhibiting a significant relationship between their area and mass. As a result of the Moon's gravitational effect, the locations where objects would find stable equilibrium in orbit around the Earth are altered. Prior studies have outlined how the Moon's influence modifies the orbits of objects that follow a specific trajectory, which are characterized by particular points of resonance. However, instead of following the traditional model, where the Moon's effect is dependent on the eccentricities of both orbits, we discovered a scenario where the Moon's effect is contingent on a measure of how flattened the Earth is. Furthermore, through numerical analysis, we investigate the circumstances under which the Moon's effect will have a significant impact on the objects' orbits.

We re-examine the trade-offs within standard tight-binding models that enable the computation of electronic responses to light. By concentrating on the two-dimensional tight-binding model and incorporating the effects of spin and light polarization, we derive a compact equation for the electric current induced by light on any tight-binding system. This explicit representation highlights the advantages of using the dipole gauge over the velocity gauge in describing light-matter interaction. Furthermore, our general framework is applicable to various light interaction phenomena, such as photoemission, entropy changes, and light-induced currents, within any tight-binding network of any dimension and complexity. Its utility is demonstrated through calculations of light-induced currents in two and three-dimensional TB systems undergoing a semiconductor-to-metal transition.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models are used for object representation, is employed along with a novel layer designed for joint shape and pose estimation. An innovative layer is developed using a differentiable correspondence matching approach to handle intra-class shape and pose variations. By using a multi-task loss function combining both shape and pose regression, our model can effectively capture the complex interactions between object shapes and poses. Through extensive testing on real-world data from novel views and rotations, our model demonstrates a significant reduction in object detection and recognition errors compared to existing approaches.

This research paper introduces a novel approach to extend the Cauchy distribution in a complex plane. It parameterizes the Cauchy distribution with two parameters, denoted as $\gamma$ and $\tau$, and shows that this parameterization maintains the distribution's invariance to scaling and rotation. A specific parameterization is chosen such that one parameter represents the radius of uncertainty in an angular sense and the other parameter controls the orientation. The paper also derives a geometric interpretation of this parameterization. In addition, it covers key aspects of the extended Cauchy distribution, including its probability density function, moment calculation, and a method to estimate the distribution from a sample of points. This methodology is anticipated to have useful applications in fields like signal processing, remote sensing, and hydrology, where situations with high levels of noise and limited data samples are encountered.

To determine the efficacy of novel treatments, basket trials enroll patients with specific genetic mutations across various cancer types. As a result, each trial arm may include patients from multiple indications. In order to optimize patient assignment and maximize statistical power, patients with certain molecular profiles should be prioritized. This can be complex due to varying levels of patient availability and uncertainty surrounding patient distribution in each trial arm. To tackle this challenge, we developed an algorithm designed to balance patient allocation across different treatment options while taking into account anticipated patient populations. This algorithm employs a simulated annealing technique to improve results, particularly in situations involving constraints. A real-world case study based on actual clinical data was used to evaluate and compare the performance of our algorithm with existing approaches.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration techniques, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that focus on overall shape alignment, PRNet is tailored for partial views and efficiently handles partial to partial matching. Key components include a robust keypoint detector for identifying stable objects features and a geometric refinement module, supported by a suite of synthetic datasets, to test its effectiveness. Notably, PRNet outperforms leading methods in point cloud registration on Oberkirler Benchmark Dataset 2018.

A group G is said to have property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G result in a twisted conjugacy class containing more than just the identity element. In this paper, we demonstrate the solvability of the problem: does every group with property $R_\infty$ embody a nilpotent class.

The top quark mass is crucial in determining the stability of the Higgs potential and electroweak symmetry breaking. Developing realistic top quark mass operators to study these phenomena at the Large Hadron Collider is essential. This work presents a comprehensive top quark mass operator that incorporates both next-to-leading order QCD corrections and electroweak effects, along with a comparison of several subtraction techniques to validate its validity. Using the top quark effective potential to quantify residual higher-order effects, we examine the residual band for the pole mass. Additionally, we simulate top quark pair production using event generator HEPEGRA v5.18.00, demonstrating the necessity of including electroweak corrections in the simulation of the process.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the combination of two norms, one being submultiplicative and the other being supermultiplicative. The nontriviality of these spaces, such as ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, depends on specific growth rate conditions of their underlying function classes. The use of Fourier transforms allows us to establish relationships between different spaces, while a decay estimate of inverse polynomial order in conjunction with smoothness is found to be necessary and sufficient for the nontriviality of one such space, ${\Sigma}^{\infty}_s$. Additionally, the article considers weighted versions of these spaces, which lead to conclusions regarding the weighted ultraspherical Hylerman spaces.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps. In this study, a Cyclic Segmentation Generative Adversarial Network is proposed that simultaneously performs domain adaptation and object identification within a single unified structure. Apart from standard CycleGAN losses and supervisory signals from labeled source domain images, additional self-supervised objectives focusing on the segmentation are employed to optimize performance utilizing target domain images devoid of manual labels. Evaluations on the segmentation of neuronal nuclei using EM images and unlabeled ExM images confirm that the proposed CySGAN outperforms not only pre-trained models but also methods that execute domain adaptation followed by segmentation in sequence. Details regarding the model implementation, newly acquired dense labels for EM images, newly collected paired datasets, additional modality combinations, and further A/B comparison studies using various models including DeepLabv3, DeepLabv3+, and Segformer are available in the supplementary material available online.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron equipped with an RBF
kernel layer to accurately forecast actions. In our experiments, Feature Mapping RNN
achieved superior performance on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction datasets
compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions such as Kepler, K2, and TESS, providing significant insights into the physical processes occurring on short-term and long-term scales in active stars. To better understand these phenomena and their implications, the Exoplanet White Light Catalogue (XWLcat) is being developed to compile a comprehensive catalogue of low-mass stars exhibiting white-light flares that includes newly discovered and previously observed exoplanets. This initiative will help in identifying potential sources of false positives in transit searches by pinpointing flares associated with these planets. As a starting point, the XWLcat catalogue began with an analysis of Kepler data by employing automated algorithms to identify 1,626,351 long-term periods and 55,661 short-term patterns in the light curves of 658 active stars. These patterns indicated that low-mass stars are more active than initially thought, with up to 90% of them displaying variability patterns. This work is further supplemented by the investigation of variability patterns in subgroups of active stars.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research also identifies a systematic collection of significant p-core p'-partitions that establish a substantial lower limit on their maximum size.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations that mimic real-world movements, such as moving around objects. To address this vulnerability, we propose an efficient technique that generates plausible point clouds while ensuring the transformed points do not deviate from their original positions. Unlike existing approaches, our method does not rely on expensive optimization or copyable features like CNNs. We achieve this effect by applying a limited number of simple operations to move points around in a way that mimics real-world movements, such as moving objects across each other. We provide detailed explanations of how our method works, which involves just three common types of movements: translating, scaling, and rotating points. As a result, we are able to train a single set of parameters that can accurately predict the effects of all these different point cloud transformations, which greatly reduces the training time. We have tested our method by simulating a variety of real-world transformations, such as moving around objects and cars, and found that it is able to accurately predict the effects of these movements by as much as 99.9%. We have also shown that by using our method, we are able to improve the robustness of point cloud transformation models against manipulations that mimic real-world movements, by as much as 97%.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease interference probabilities. We introduce a clear channel assessment process, known as medium sensing, for detecting narrowband interference and present a dynamic ALOHA protocol based on this assessment. In CSMA, we present a geometric modeling approach to analyze average transmission attempts and interference probabilities per radar unit. We introduce a new metric to gauge performance and compare ALOHA and CSMA efficiency. We observe that FMCW radar network transmission behaves differently from typical wireless communication patterns and present a dynamic ALOHA protocol to minimize transmission attempts and mitigate interference. To compare ALOHA and CSMA performance, we introduce a new metric to gauge performance and conduct numerical analysis to determine efficient transmission parameters. We discover that CSMA outperforms ALOHA in most cases and present a potential improvement to the clear channel assessment process for future research.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. A supporting model portrays the sample as an energy-preserving spectral filter, aligning with the observed results and providing insight into the entangled two-photon absorption process. By combining cutting-edge quantum interference techniques with a detailed mathematical framework, this work presents an innovative perspective on ETPA research.

The complex projective space CP(V) is defined as the set of all complex lines in the finite-dimensional complex vector space V, equipped with a specific topology. Similarly, the complex Grassmannian manifold G(2, V) represents the set of all two-dimensional complex subspaces within V, also possessing a specific topology. This research paper investigates the topological properties of mappings between the complex projective space CP(V) and the complex Grassmannian manifold G(2, V), specifically demonstrating that an expression can be formulated in terms of a standard topological space, and providing evidence that shows the existence of non-trivial topological structures in this context.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, this study incorporates time-aware decomposition models to fulfill
this need. In particular, this work presents a novel time-aware knowledge graph
factorization model capable of learning temporal patterns by leveraging low-rank
factorized time representations. To establish a comprehensive time-aware
decomposition framework, this study also develops low-rank factorization models
for individual knowledge graph components, including pointwise, pairwise, and
multirelation models. By extending the generative model of existing knowledge graph
embeddings, this study further formalizes time-aware knowledge graph embeddings
and provides necessary generative model inference strategies. Experimental evaluations
on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed time-aware
knowledge graph factorization models, yielding superior results compared to existing
time-aware embedding models.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, the ground sound is examined, and a model is developed to simulate it under various impact conditions. By analyzing the sound wave propagation through the ground, the full waveform is captured, and it's found that its spectral characteristics are unaffected, whereas its temporal pattern is determined by factors such as soil type, the size and depth of the impact, and the speed at which the object penetrates the ground. To generate audible ground sounds, the amplitude of the waveform must be above a threshold, and this model enables the creation of rig-compatible sounds that can be used in realistic audio simulations.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-perfect correlations. This research aims to clarify the concept of non-perfect correlations using the framework of projection operators, demonstrates a new form of "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof based on this concept, and also explores its connection to the box world in quantum reality models.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these flat bands within M$_2$X$_2$S$_2$L$_2$ materials ($M$ = Mo, W; $X$ = P, As, $L$ = S, Se, Te) expose key roles of interlayer and intralayer interactions. We investigate the stability of these materials by examining lattice deformations and estimating associated energies. Our calculations using the evolutionary algorithm for structure prediction identify multiple micropercyberic flat band systems within this class of materials, featuring high carrier densities and potential applications in superconducting, magnetic, and optoelectronic technologies.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Our findings indicate that hydrogen boride monolayer possesses intermediate direct and indirect gaps in its phonon spectrum, as well as electron-phonon coupling strengths exceeding 2.0, justifying its classification as a strong superconductor. Applying Allen-Coorden's method to analyze charge density, we've determined that hydrogen and boron contribute most significantly to the electron-phonon interaction. Our results predict that this material could achieve superconductivity at temperatures between 10-40 K under optimal doping conditions.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here coincidentally relate to the numbers A124324 in the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. A distinct counting method is developed for these numbers, and we establish a one-to-one correspondence between a specific type of division and the division of quantities into fewer equal parts. Furthermore, we prove that our counting method aligns with a broader combinatorial approach involving the division of quantities into n equal parts. Lastly, we investigate how to divide quantities into n equal parts where certain items have restricted distributions, and we establish a formula for counting these divisions.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups using ergodic measures, which represents the group's stiffness in relation to these measures. This stiffness is quantified through a mathematical formula involving various elements, including specific characteristics of the group's action. By analyzing the characteristics of this formula, we're able to determine the group's stiffness in relation to various ergodic measures, such as those resulting from arithmetic groups and measures that are invariant under certain rotations. Additionally, we're able to demonstrate that the group's stiffness is not necessarily influenced by its characteristics, but rather depends on the properties of the group action.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that identifies and overrules faulty components. To mitigate the impact of computational errors in the arbitration logic itself, a fail-safe strategy is implemented, ensuring system operation even in such scenarios. To prevent accidents, a risk control module assesses potential hazards and suggests appropriate actions to the backup system. To ensure the effectiveness of this design in ensuring public safety, a rigorous analysis of potential failures and their consequences is carried out. Based on this examination, appropriate measures are taken to minimize risks and ensure the reliability of the design.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence between components. This framework is applied to an artificial Markov model and real-world data from diverse fields, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting clusters across various contexts.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes. Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). To address these debates, this paper delves into the underlying metaphysics that Leibniz envisioned for his calculus, uncovering philosophical metaphysical assumptions in the process. By examining Leibniz's metaphysics through the lens of Rescher's modal syllogistic, it becomes clear that the best representation of Leibnizian calculus is actually the Robbins-Reynolds framework, which is a reformulation of SIA with added metaphysical features. While the metaphysical aspects of this framework may not align with the prevailing understanding of the calculus as a classical mathematics, a case can be made for its metaphysical coherence.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using data from future surveys such as Square Kilometre Array. We develop a likelihood calculation for this data, taking into account uncertainties and how they interact with different parameters. We then apply this likelihood to mock data from a specific SKA project, and find the expected errors for key parameters such as the matter density and Hubble constant. We also use the EFT approach to analyze a real data set and compare it to results from a simpler model, finding some discrepancies but generally supporting previously published findings.

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the dimension of the sequence's vector space is infinite. In our research, we derive this result as a specific instance of a more comprehensive model-theoretic finding. Then, focusing on vector spaces, we demonstrate that if a condition such as $T(e_i)=e_{\phi(i)}$ is to replace the previous operator assumption, $\phi$ must be equivalent to the successor function, defined as incrementing a number by 1. Finally, we explore analogs of these concepts within division ring spaces and polynomial space sequences.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have achieved notable success in enhancing recommendation accuracy. Although effective, these strategies have a significant drawback as they fail to consider user preferences individually, instead applying a universal understanding to all users. Consequently, recommendations may appear irrelevant to users in cases where documents are recommended. To address this issue, a novel unified framework called UCDM is proposed, combining user preference modeling with document modeling to optimize the recommendation process. The proposed framework utilizes low-rank user and document factorization along with a joint optimization of their target variables. Moreover, a proposed method called user guided denoising auto-encoder for embedding denoising is also implemented to enhance the quality of the recommended results by integrating the recommended information. The proposed framework's performance is evaluated on two real-world datasets, demonstrating superior performance to existing techniques.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$. It is suggested that the primary
cause of isospin breaking arises from different transition matrix elements of
$\pi^0$ and $\eta$ rather than the matrix element of the scalar glueball, and
that the $SU(3)$ decoupling approximation is reasonably valid for these
processes. As a consequence, the contributions from loop processes involving
$\rho^0$ and $\omega$ are essentially equivalent, and the ratio of the decay
widths is primarily determined by the transition matrix elements of the mesons
$\pi^0$, $\eta$, and $\eta'$, which can be reliably calculated using the
quark model. Based on these considerations, the expected decay width for the
$a_0(980)$ meson is $ \mathcal O(10^{-8})$ eV, in keeping with LHCb findings
consisting of a rate upper limit of $1.46 \times 10^{-5}$.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers to pinpoint the phase diversity signature b) a focal plane tracker uses the intrinsic speckle pattern of a testplate to localize the field of view, while c) a wavefront sensor uses a supercontinuum source to refine the system's sensitivity d) and a spatial scanner, utilizing the intrinsic speckle pattern again, determines the orientation of the beams. Featuring 30 nm/pixel pixel sensors, the camera boasts high spatial resolution and sensitivity, along with rapid 13 Hz readout speed. Leveraging these advanced features allows for the accurate identification and tracking of the beams, facilitating successful acquisition of the GRAVITY instrument.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields efficient parameterized schemes for specific problem types, such as the $k$-Center and Leiserson Centers. Conversely, for the Leiserson Center with Outliers, we discover a contrasting result, demonstrating no efficient parameterized scheme exists for a specific variant and conjecturing a similar scenario for other problem types.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system, as well as a bound on error growth. We develop an online algorithm achieving the lowest possible evaluation count, which is a function of these parameters. This research further includes an analysis of error bounds and recovery accuracy. While the problem can be challenging over general fields, we prove that our approach remains feasible for specific types of fields, such as finite fields and transcendental fields.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a combination of light-matter interactions and is enabled in the absence of a driving field. The system exhibits a transition from a protected even photon state to a composite light-matter superposition. The emissions of odd photons are prevented due to a difference in amplitude and phase between the light-matter superposition and its mirror image. The parity symmetry of the system remains intact despite the introduction of imperfections in the cavity frequency and Jaynes-Cummings coupling strength. However, variations in the Rabi coupling strength between the qubit and the cavity affect the frequency of the super-Rabi oscillations and alter the photon number correlation in odd photons emissions. The preservation of photon bundle emission under perturbations in the qubit and cavity fields is a key feature of this phenomenon. The realization of this phenomenon is achievable using superconducting quantum circuits with existing technologies and may lead to the discovery of new protected states in complex quantum systems.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and involves straightforward computation by each node in each round.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, accurately modeling the interaction between gravitational fields and various forms of matter is crucial. This work focuses on developing and implementing an approach for distributing the stress-energy components of matter across a grid without being constrained to a specific, fixed configuration. We introduce a novel method for modifying an initial conditions protocol that takes into account the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints, ensuring that the simulation adapts to desired patterns of stress-energy without being bound by arbitrary, constant states. We further demonstrate a method for developing a recovery algorithm that utilizes non-linear combinations of gravitational field components to recover the original, complex distribution of matter from a constrained, uniform state. We showcase the effectiveness of this approach through a set of examples, including a scenario of a rotating black hole surrounded by a accretion disk.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. To achieve this goal, the experiment relies on accurately understanding various components affecting its measurement, including instrumental factors and external influences such as the Earth's interior. To address these challenges, the experiment requires a comprehensive data acquisition system. Described here are the design and implementation specifics of this system's hardware, including its roles, requirements, and key technical decisions made during development.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and health monitoring, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. Nevertheless, addressing this challenge is complicated due to the extensive future context required for accurate predictions, which significantly increases the complexity as the look-ahead time grows. Current approaches using Transformer architectures are limited by their inability to effectively utilize distant information, resulting in decreasing accuracy as the look-ahead time increases, and they often rely on speculative techniques like model ensembling to compensate for these limitations. Furthermore, their training is hindered by the extensive look-ahead time-dependent data requirements, which are often in short supply. 
To address these challenges, we propose an advanced attention mechanism known as Forest Transformer (ForExT), consisting of multiple layer networks with unique properties, to tackle long sequence time-series forecasting more effectively. By employing a dynamic attention weighted recurrent layer at the forefront to capture time dependencies and a nested Transformer layer at the back to extract features and minimize look-ahead time dependencies, ForExT outperforms existing state-of-the-art models by an impressive margin. To enhance performance further, we introduce a Forest Layer, an ensemble of recurrent state-aware fully connected layers with delayers, utilizing accumulated feature state across time and backforest features respectively, thus making ForExT a forest-inspired model. Moreover, our approach is adaptable and can be applied to both data-poor and data-rich scenarios with practical applications.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. This distortion causes images of celestial objects to be misaligned and makes calculations of coordinates and magnitudes unreliable. The Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector corrects this issue by employing a prism or wedge designed to refract light equally across various wavelengths. The specific design requirements for such correctors depend on factors like atmospheric conditions, telescope latitude, and operational wavelengths. Typically, researchers calculate the required angle of correction through complex mathematical formulas incorporating these variables. In this project, we applied the Python programming language to efficiently calculate and display the desired angle of correction under different scenarios, utilizing it in a graphical user interface to aid users.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range, but can actually be searching for much broader ranges. A network of sensors, by cross-correlating their measurements over time, can detect this low-frequency fluctuations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range, but can actually searching for much broader ranges. This low-frequency fluctuations can be detected using existing sensors, and is within range of what is feasible with upcoming sensors to detect.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through a constrained optimization problem. A unique and highly efficient algorithm is presented to solve this optimization problem, which yields highly accurate results for large values of Kc. The uniqueness of solutions and the stability of these solutions in relation to the sampling grid size and the truncation frequency Kc are also investigated. Several two-dimensional imaging scenarios are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in practice.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being widely adopted in various switch development projects. Despite the popularity of the P4-Linux framework, which allows running native P4 programs on Linux hosts, there is a lack of comprehensive analysis of its overheads. This study involves developing a benchmark suite consisting of 28 short programs and 8 long programs to measure the computational overheads introduced by the P4-Linux framework when executing in-user-space. The results show that P4 programs experience varying levels of overhead when run out-of-user-space, with average overheads ranging from 7% to 261% for short programs and 14% to 106% for long programs when compared to in-user-space execution. Furthermore, a long program experiencing 261% overhead can still maintain high throughput, at 85% of the original value, indicating that the impact of P4-Linux overhead on switch performance is generally tolerable.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that utilize higher-order function spaces to project transport errors, thereby enhancing the transport scheme's accuracy without requiring correspondingly high resolutions for the underlying mesh. One approach involves a stable and convergent projection technique using a specially structured mixed finite element space; the other method relies on a stable and convergent continuous-space projection that splines onto a higher-order space while utilizing a continuous-space projection operator. Both methods can be easily adapted for use with alternative transport schemes that incorporate different discretization techniques, such as semi-Lagrange or flux-closure methods. We demonstrate the implementation and convergence of these methods in a range of simulations involving both smooth and chaotic flows.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

A three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is examined, which consists of a chaotic non-Wada basin surrounded by three-spheres with full boundary dissipation. Numerical results show that when weak dissipation occurs, non-Wada basins gain stability and an invariant boundary is formed, which shrinks over time, ultimately isolating the surviving basin from the three-spheres. This boundary is homeostatic, exhibiting a unique property where the flow across it is uniformly zero in all directions. This research provides theoretical and numerical evidence supporting the theoretical predictions of a previous paper.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various combinations of the associated parameters, focusing particularly on the scenario where the decay of the intermediate scalar occurs before it is confined back to a brane.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes and confirm that the singularity at the center is hidden by an event horizon, thus validating the second law of thermodynamics. The validity of the third law of thermodynamics is verified by examining the properties of extremal black holes. The validity of the cosmic censorship conjecture is confirmed by demonstrating that non-extremal black hole horizons always exist, thus effectively hiding the singularity at the center. The impact of a massive anti-de Sitter universe on the thermodynamic properties and the structure of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes is also investigated, where the introduction of a finite universe reduces the mass and charge of the black holes, but does not change their signature.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated.
