The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

The thread of open questions and insights in metals dates back to the 1960s, marking a significant period in time. The decade saw significant advancements in the study of metals, yet key issues persisted. This time saw the emergence of Kadanoff Baym Green's functional methods in theoretical modeling. The 1970s witnessed considerable growth in theoretical research on metals. The time saw a surge in the study of correlated metals, facilitated by the advent of quantum Monte Carlo techniques. The 1980s marked a period of heightened controversy in the study of metals. The time saw a rise in the consideration of non-equilibrium phenomena in metals. The 1990s witnessed considerable advancements in the theoretical and experimental study of metals at high temperatures. The time saw a rise in the consideration of dynamic properties of metals. The 2000s saw a rise in the study of metals in the presence of external fields. The time saw a rise in the consideration of nano-scale metals. The period from 2010 saw a rise in the consideration of nano-scale metals undergoing colossal changes, inspired by cutting-edge experiments.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed microstate thermodynamics aligns with the expected outcomes from ideal gas theories. Moreover, we've discovered that the direction of energy transfer relative to temperature differences follows the conventional signs, and the total energy exerted by the expanding system surpasses the work performed by the walls, leading to positive net work production.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for the underlying connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by extremely high amplitudes, in slightly inhomogeneous Hertzian chains. These phenomena arise from initial conditions creating "notches" in the energy landscape, leading to isolated patterns of time-dependent oscillations. Mathematical analysis involves the use of Geometric Integration techniques, specifically compatible numerical integrators, to validate the analytical predictions of the nanopton profile, and assess its stability over time. Numerical results indicate that the notch shape significantly influences the magnitude of the nanopton, and that these waves may move under certain conditions. Ultimately, we investigate the dynamics of multiple notches, demonstrating the emergence of complex interactions and interactions that result in the destruction of the nanopton.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signal of colliding particles is typically hidden within gravitational waves. Our analysis explores the potential for observing the effects of colliding particles through measurable patterns in primordial non-gaussian corrections to the cosmological gravitational wave background. The signal of colliding particles can create resonance-like patterns in certain inflationary scenarios, such as models with heavy scalars or additional fields. These patterns may manifest as distinct, oscillatory features in field fluctuations or gravitational waves, whose characteristics can provide insight into the properties of the colliding particles. The features of collision signals can be dissected into two components: one related to the collision itself, and another related to the oscillatory mode of the field that mediates the collision. The collision signal is maximized when the energy of the colliding particles equals the oscillation frequency, a condition met more easily in scenarios with heavy scalar fields. Our analysis considers various observable signals across different frequencies, such as through corrections to equilateral non-gaussian corrections, through post-inflationary effects like ultra-violet instability, through specific features in inflationary models, through specific features in post-inflationary scenarios, through signal of colliding particles through a different field, through signal of colliding particles through a different field II, through a different signal of colliding particles through a different field III, through a different signal

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching of K_G. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization next. In our work, a class of quartic graphs called accordion graphs is defined, parameterized by n and k, which we designate as A[n,k]. We find that a specific family of infinite quartic (also circulant) graphs which exhibit the PH-property belong to the class of accordion graphs. They are derived from circulant graphs of type $(\sqrt{p}, \sqrt{p+1})$ for any prime number p greater than 2, which resolves the unknownness of circulant graphs with the PH-property for any prime number p greater than 2. It's noted that an infinite family of quartic graphs which have the PH-property but are not circulant can be constructed using a technique of folding an appropriate subgraph of a planar graph that contains a large enough number of vertices.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ to cause the wavepacket to experience periodic fluctuations between two trajectories. The critical parameter $\theta_c$ determines the extent of wavepacket spreading in a logarithmic time scale. Two distinct limiting cases are examined - when $\theta \rightarrow 0$ and when $\theta \to \pi$, resulting in different spreading behaviors. Under the latter condition, the wavepacket exhibits a unique "dipping" behavior distinct from previous logarithmic spreading observations.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely excel at handling complex, intra-class relationships within semantic segments. In contrast, previously established differences between ViT and convnets were mainly attributed to the former's superior representation capabilities. Building on this insight, we developed a straightforward, patch-based self-supervised method called Self-Supervised Multi-scale Patch Association (SSMPA). SSMPA employs a novel, multi-scale average pooling technique to enhance the spatial utilization of ViT features. Our experiments on ImageNet and Pascal Context demonstrate that integrating SSMPA into ViT architectures consistently yields significantly higher semantic segmentation accuracies compared to existing self-supervised approaches. Notably, even when evaluated in a fully supervised setting, our results reveal substantial advantages of combining self-supervised ViT features with fine-tuning over the corresponding convolutional networks.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is independent of time. Our analysis reveals a vast universe dominated by the dark fluid model, with its dynamics governed by a system of nonlinear differential equations. Our research suggests that the model exhibits chaotic behavior, as indicated by a diverging phase space, and our findings support this conclusion. However, we have discovered a stable island. Our study could provide insight into the dark energy problem if we were to modify the model slightly to eliminate its dissipative nature.

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for incompressible Euler equations with bounded initial data has a critical issue. This demonstrates the non-existence of solutions for certain initial and boundary conditions in related partial differential equation problems.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their ability to create highly realistic images, often referred to as "images from text". However, generating images with specific semantic details remains challenging, a problem that limits their ability to create images based on natural language inputs. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that allows us to incorporate image editing abilities into image generation, conditioning the process on both text and image inputs. This enables not only the creation of images from text but also the editing of existing images with text guidance. Our method employs a simple yet effective technique to align the semantic content of untrained and trained images, using a fixed set of image embeddings as a bridge. Through extensive experiments and visual evaluations, we demonstrate the ability of our model to perform various image editing tasks while maintaining the preservation of original image features. Additionally, we showcase the ability of our model to generate high-quality images from text.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation in achieving reversible steganography involves accurate predictive modeling that distinguishes between certain and uncertain data. While deep neural networks can learn to predict probabilities of class assignments with some accuracy, they often fail to effectively distinguish between certain and uncertain predictions. This research aims to apply Bayesian deep learning principles in order to disentangle two types of uncertainty - predictive uncertainty related to class predictions and posterior uncertainty resulting from model inference. We successfully implement a simple approach using Gaussian Mixture Models to differentiate between certain and uncertain predictions and demonstrate its application in enabling label-informed reversible steganography on standard datasets, thereby achieving improved coverage and capacity metrics while also reducing the overall steagoographic capacity by a factor of 2.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by employing phenomenological approaches and modeling neutrino and dark matter properties with appropriate form factors. We found that J/ψ decay into invisible matter visible through a photon can be detected by experiments such as BELLE II and LHCb with significant statistical power. We looked at the impact of this experiment on form factor constraints and new parameter spaces including dark photons, a new boson, and a type of scalar or pseudoscalar dark matter component. Our research also shows that J/ψ decay into invisible matter visible through a photon offers a strong statistical advantage over other searches for sub-GeV mass dark matter.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, that play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's intricate phenomena. These points, detected in numerous studies, are considered essential for modeling the solar atmosphere's heat dissipation. This research aims to examine the size distribution of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere and compare it to similar observations in the chromosphere layers. Using observed data from the Hinode SOT, this study analyzes magnetic bright points of varying polarities, characterizing their distributions in terms of area, diameter, and specific magnetic field features. The results show that magnetic bright points adhere to a power-law distribution for area and diameter measurements, with stronger fields linked to smaller structures and a distinct disparity in size between magnetic field strengths.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities. This study delves into the constraints on such monopoles utilizing galaxy halo ellipticity observations, as well as those from the Milky Way's inner region, to establish a lower limit on the cross-section of dark sector interactions based on monopole mass, with monopole masses less than $10^{-3}$ GeV constrained by halo observations and those in the Milky Way's inner region, with monopole masses less than $10^{-5}$ GeV. Additionally, this study's findings on the monopole lifetime offer improved constraints compared to previously made assumptions.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging video transformer technology to analyze time-series data from multiple sources, such as satellite imagery and weather monitoring systems. A video Swin-Transformer is applied to gather insights from the dynamics within consecutive weather image frames. Experimental validation using the simple yet effective WeatherSynth dataset has yielded remarkable results, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach in predicting weather patterns with accuracy.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the possibility of dark matter in $SU(3)_C \otimes SU(2)_L \otimes U(1)_Y$ models with an additional $Z_2$ symmetry, under the transformation $(L, \lambda, H)\to (-1)^F (L, \lambda, H)$, where $L$ and $\lambda$ are components of $SU(2)_L \otimes U(1)_Y$ doublets and singlets, respectively, and $F$ is the fermion number. We investigate a scenario where the scalar potential possesses both $Z_2$-breaking (isomorphic to $U(1)_X$ with $X=I_3(3\lambda_1)+(B-\mu_2)^2$, where $B$ and $\mu_2$ are components of $SU(2)_L$ and $U((1)_Y$ triplets, respectively) and demonstrate that a sum of linear terms with $Z_2$-breaking coefficients can be optimized to a single linear combination, thus defining a model with one viable dark matter candidate and another scalar singlet that may be the Higgs boson. We compute the mass spectra and couplings of the model and further investigate the possibility of dark matter direct detection, where

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling proper neuron function and survival. Disruption of this process is linked to various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons coordinate transportation to target vulnerable areas. We investigate how a complex neuron geometry influences the delivery of substances by simulating microtubal transport dynamics. Our models reveal that neurons employ different strategies to prioritize transport based on the structure and location of their branches. We propose a decision-making process that allows ends of microtubules to act as traffic managers, regulating the arrival of cargo at distant locations by adjusting the speed of individual molecular motors. We demonstrate that these models accurately match experimental observations of transport patterns, and provide insights into the critical roles of microtubule ends in neuronal function.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We also present a method for generating genuine banking transaction graphs via randomization. The outcome of our preliminary analysis indicates that extracting network motifs can reveal meaningful and understandable patterns within the data.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, emitting signals across various frequency spectrums, including gamma-rays, X-rays, and gravitational waves. We analyze the emitted spectrum and find that the high-energy electromagnetic emissions far exceed those predicted by standard accretion models. Furthermore, the intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation could potentially be detectable by space-based observatories, such as the Gamma-ray Observatory and LIGO/Virgo.

Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of weak electromagnetic interactions rely on form factors to describe the hadronic part of the final states, which can be further understood by decomposing the hadronic current into specific orbital angular momentum components. Given the increasing data availability from future experiments, a new description of the hadronic currents is presented, using the isobar model to describe the three-body decay processes. These descriptions can facilitate the investigation of weak electromagnetic interactions and the properties of particles and nuclei.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ represents a normalization factor and $\beta$ represents a similarity threshold. Initially developed by Tversky (1977), these models aim to counterintuitive effects of human memory errors. These error effects are due, in part, to a phenomenon called "gradient effect," where gradual retrieval of information is preferred over discrete retrieval. Under certain conditions, $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ becomes a metric known as "Jensen distance" when $\alpha$ equals 1 and $\beta$ equals 1. We demonstrate that $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a semimetric when $\alpha$ is not equal to 0, even when $\beta$ is greater than 1. Additionally, we establish a method to determine a unique value for $\alpha$ so that $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ is a semimetric with specific properties. This parameter is equivalent to the sum of all weights in a given set. By analyzing $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ through the lens of semimetric theory, we hope to better understand its potential in addressing the gradient effect.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired data to transform blurry images into clear ones. However, creating synthetic blurry data required for these models is costly and impractical with limited available datasets. To overcome this limitation, we propose an innovative method for generating blurry data without needing a clear counterpart, using real-world blurry images and an on-the-fly derived motion field. To make the most of limited training data, we employ self-supervision and a compact model design efficiently learning from the generated data. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in motion deblurring performance, with particular success when only a limited amount of training data is available. Our code and models can be found at https://github.com/ghamiar/MMDB.

Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of exhibiting autonomous Hebbian learning through multiple input channels. This artificial neural network model is built using autowaves and adaptive molecules and can recognize patterns in the input data. The study demonstrates its effectiveness by applying it to a complex problem, decoding genetic information stored in DNA sequences, and shows that it can learn and generalize accurately.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill this property. To explore this relationship, we examine specific properties of sets within the ultrapower of ordered sets, particularly those that are dense and co-dense, and use these findings to understand the set of all ultrafilters within a particular Cartesian product of finite sets.

Scientific datasets are diverse in terms of their structure and associated costs. The process of evaluating computational models according to the standards set by dataset requirements can be costly. Typically, models are assessed based on their performance in predicting key dataset variables. The challenge here is that the cost of validating models is directly related to the cost of collecting dataset variables. Our study focuses on developing an approach where models are ranked according to their predicted values of dataset variables, taking into account the cost of variable collection. We introduce a new method called Theoretical Expected Ranking (TER) that utilizes core dataset properties, such as the distribution of collection costs and variable dependencies. TER is proven to accurately identify the optimal model ranking when collection costs are uniformly distributed and additive. Furthermore, TER is shown to be a good approximation of the optimal ranking in non-uniform cost scenarios. Our approach also considers the limitations of finite dataset resources and develops a iterative process for computing TER on such datasets. We propose several algorithms based on TER and evaluate their effectiveness using real-world dataset examples.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with a chromatic number of t is composed of t-colorable subgraphs. This has been reinforced by a more stringent conjecture proposing that every such graph includes a complete graph with t vertices within it. This more stringent conjecture has been reinforced by yet another claim which posits that every such graph includes a complete graph with t vertices that is also entirely contained within a linear structure. This more stringent conjecture has been proven for graphs that are planar or close to being planar, which has significant implications for the coloring of general graphs. By analyzing the structure of coloring numbers in relation to the presence of certain types of structures within them, the proof reveals that the more stringent conjecture is true for graphs that are close to being planar. This is achieved by showing that any graph with a high coloring number but minimal degree must contain a complete graph with a high number of vertices that is also contained within a linear structure, which is then used to prove the more stringent conjecture for all graphs with a high coloring number.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized low-rank representation. We model this signal recovery as an convex optimization problem, formulating it as a regularized least squares objective with a kernel-based term. This problem can be broken down into a series of smaller optimization tasks, each defined on a specific edge of the graph, and we develop an adaptive algorithm accordingly. We show that this algorithm is capable of achieving optimal results in a limited number of iterations, and provide theoretical proof of its performance characteristics. Additionally, we conduct extensive numerical experiments to evaluate the algorithm's efficacy across various graph topologies and noise types.

Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial disturbance as a trigger, as opposed to vacuum fluctuations, yields superior results despite reduced entanglement. Our findings have implications for optimizing entangled atomic state production for quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry applications.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants. We derive sharp estimates for this eigenvalue problem when the exponent $p$ lies between 1 and infinity. This work generalizes previous research on the first Robin eigenvalue, and provides new insights into the behavior of this eigenvalue in different functional contexts.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs represent this process through a set of weighted, directionally-oriented protocols that balance new information with existing knowledge.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

This paper delves into the realm of CPT (Compositional Pattern Theory) and its expanded query type, CFI (Compositional Forest Inquiry), which builds upon CPT by incorporating path-based questions. Our investigation centers around the CFI-query's definability within specific graph classes, with a particular focus on its relationship to monadic safety and gluability. Ultimately, we explore the CFI-query's general definability within the realm of CPT.

In a compound known for spin-orbit-driven topological order, Eu2Ir2O7, 
moderate levels of Bi^4+ doping into the compound create a state of electron
conduction while preserving spin-orbit coupling. Using angle-resolved photoemission 
spectroscopy, we studied the electronic properties close to the Fermi energy and 
observed novel quasi-particle states. Our theoretical calculations using a
single-band tight-binding model suggest that the driving force behind these 
changes is the interaction between Bi ions and Ir ions, interacting in a weakly
coupled system. This interaction has a strong impact on the electronic bands,
causing them to bend and shift due to the formation of a highly correlated 
semi-metallic state with an energy gap at the Fermi energy. This discovery 
represents a new pathway to creating topological materials with an energy gap.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$, with a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the nonempty closed convex subsets of $X$. In this paper, we investigate the existence and continuous selection of Lipschitz mappings for the set-valued mapping $F$. Specifically, we demonstrate the existence of a Lipschitz continuous selection for $F$ that meets the following criteria: it is defined on the entire metric space ${\mathcal M}$, its Lipschitz constant is $L$, and it agrees with $F$ at every point in a given metric subspace ${\mathcal N}$.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple as 'cyclic' as a function $T_n$ and prove that $T_3$ is continuous and has a range exceeding 0, but also establish that $T_4$ and $T_5$ are constant at 0. Furthermore, a 1963 hypothesis proposed by Friedman presents a conjecture about the n-tuple's properties, which we demonstrate is accurate for the lower bounds of n equal to 3, 4, or 5.

Many software systems have adjustable settings through run-time options, such as logging levels and network settings, allowing users to modify them to optimize performance or meet specific demands. A system's optimal configuration is often a balance of meeting functional requirements and minimizing unnecessary features to improve efficiency. In this paper, we explore how reducing a system's adjustable settings to a specific task or scenario affects its overall behavior, including both functional and non-functional aspects. We develop a method to identify the impact of trimming system options and demonstrate its applicability through case studies on two widely used open-source systems, Apache HTTP and MySQL. Our analysis shows that stripping system options can lead to a substantial reduction in memory consumption, as well as other benefits such as decreased binary size and improved performance, without compromising the system's core capabilities.

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge. But if the recoil of a struck nucleus leads to electron ionization, even if the recoil itself is too subtle to be measured, it could still be possible to detect the released electrons. This process has been found to significantly boost the sensitivity of direct detection experiments to sub-GeV dark matter. In the present, experiments set global records, and future experiments are likely to reach the cross-sections critical to understanding thermal equilibrium.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system, involving a time-varying
coupling and Rabi oscillations. The study finds that in this interaction system,
two distinct pathways can lead to the generation of maximally entangled states,
and this entanglement remains stable for a specific range of Rabi oscillation
amplitudes. The research further discovers that by adjusting the Rabi oscillation
amplitude, it is possible to switch between different entangled states,
demonstrating a level of control that could be useful in quantum information
applications.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases by detecting subtle changes in heart rate variability. However, ECG signals can be affected by noise from various sources such as motion during sports activities. Existing noise removal techniques have limited effectiveness in filtering real-world data, prompting the need for an improved method. This study proposes a multi-stage approach that utilizes wavelet transform and phase-space pre-processing to enhance the quality of beat-to-beat intervals. The results show a significant improvement in several performance metrics, demonstrating the method's potential to accurately estimate HRV in various environments. The method's effectiveness is validated through comparison with established techniques and further verified by calculating HRV features to demonstrate its reliability.

We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done using a simplified model and further supported by simulations. The results show that the rate function has a distinct form for the confined case, which is a combination of a Gaussian function and an exponentially decreasing term, whereas for the free case, it solely consists of a Gaussian function. Additionally, the study finds that the variance of the rate function for the confined case is less than that of the free case.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture high-definition footage of 772 individuals, representing various demographics and styles. Using these multi-view images, we apply advanced 3D mesh modeling to accurately reconstruct and represent diverse human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. The proposed dataset demonstrates exceptional efficiency in learning and reconstructing a complete human model, effectively supplementing existing human body expression datasets such as MPII-Gaze, Multi-PIE, Human3.6M, and Panoptic Studio datasets, which were previously limited to single viewpoints or fewer subjects. Based on HUMBI, we develop and present a novel gaze prediction learning strategy that outperforms existing gaze estimation methods. Additionally, we demonstrate that HUMBI-driven models exhibit enhanced generalization capabilities in modeling and predicting gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations. The HUMBI dataset is made available for public access along with corresponding model architectures, training data, and data points. The code can be found at: https://github.com/IndigoIndigo/HUMBI.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming. We propose a universal framework that allows us to transfer neural models from English to other languages with minimal additional resources, choosing OOV words not in the target language's dictionary. Our results show that with just a small amount of adaptation, our method can effectively translate models between languages, and that this adaptation can be accomplished using words from a related language with a minimal amount of unknown words, eliminating the need for target language data. We tested our method with Hindi and Korean and found that it significantly outperformed other techniques. We also found that by incorporating data from a language that is both related to and dissimilar to the target language, our method can effectively handle cases where the source and target languages have very different vocabularies.

Video super-resolution is a complex task that benefits from accurate temporal frameworks.
Our model, VRSEN, addresses this challenge by leveraging a multi-scale deep network to establish
temporal connections and enhancing its accuracy through bidirectionalderivative-based frame propagation.
Furthermore, VRSEN incorporates a flexible deformable alignment module that adapts to input
resolution, maintaining consistency across scales and flow rates. By combining these approaches, we achieve
remarkable results, outperforming existing models in terms of visual quality and accuracy, particularly for
high-resolution outputs.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving multiple tasks. While it's true that
being trained on a variety of related tasks can lead to better results, it's not
always possible to have those tasks available. To overcome this limitation, we've
developed a new method that allows an agent to extract useful shared
representations directly from its experience. By doing so, we enable the
agent to take full advantage of being able to handle a variety of tasks. We
implement this approach in a new multi-task reinforcement learning method,
which we then test on a range of scenarios and compare it to established
methods.

We investigate the performance of heat engines driven by time-varying temperatures and heating powers for explicitly defined time intervals. Our research focuses on a two-spin system separated by a non-conspiring heat engine that converts the thermal energy discrepancy into useful electrical energy. Both the system and heat bath temperatures, as well as the Prando process's temperature scaling parameter, are subject to strict time limitations. Our goal is to identify the most efficient working periods within these time constraints and examine how the duration of these periods affects their efficiency. Our analysis shows that the maximum possible efficiency is represented by a continuous function, known as the Helmholtz coefficient, which itself has multiple extrema. These extrema occur when the system reaches thermal equilibrium with the heat bath. Our findings are verified using both analytical and numerical methods.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We introduce a group of nonlinear transformations known as the generalized heterochaos baker maps, which encompass the classic Grebogi-May baker map and its variant, the Birkhoff-Pufik generalized Grebogi-May baker map. These variants exhibit unique properties such as smooth changes in ergodic properties and transition to chaos. A new class of parameters is identified that distinguishes the conservative and dissipative dynamics of these maps, making them ideal for modeling a wide range of physical phenomena. By applying the Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser theory, we're able to describe the invariant sets of these maps in detail, including the structure of their exact point sets, which motivate future research into the geometric properties of these sets.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. The Higgs boson discovery has heightened interest in the scalar sector of nature. Researchers have identified a critical gap in our understanding, specifically within the second generation of particles, where there is currently no experimental data available. The presence of flavor-changing neutral currents (FCNCs), such as processes involving b-quarks transitioning to lighter s-quarks, makes the search for these reactions both challenging and necessary. Given the significant sensitivity improvements anticipated from upcoming experiments, particularly those involving beam-dump experiments and future lepton colliders, it is crucial to undertake in-depth theoretical studies in preparation. This paper undertakes a comprehensive analysis of the sensitivity to the parameter space of a second generation of particles in the Standard Model and its extensions through measurement of exclusive Zbb̄ processes at a high-energy electron collider. The research considers a range of realistic detector scenarios to determine the potential to detect a second generation of particles at such a collider.

This paper presents a generative model called Fast Spectrogram Network (FSN), which generates audio waveforms from spectral representations using a pitch-dependent dilated convolutional neural network approach. The Spectrogram Network (SN) utilizes stacked dilated convolution layers to analyze spectral features at varying frequencies and lengths. The pitch-dependent FSN variant adapts the convolutional layers by adjusting the dilation factor based on predicted pitch values. The model is trained in two stages: first, it's optimized to reproduce a standard training dataset, and then it's fine-tuned to generate new audio samples while minimizing post-processing errors. The FSN method demonstrates significant post-processing improvements over existing approaches like WaveNet and the parallel Gated CNN in pitch-constrained generative scenarios.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendation data shortages, and their vulnerability to irregular patterns in consumer behavior. In response to these challenges, researchers integrated Machine Learning techniques into CF to enhance its predictive power and robustness. This integration brought about a new wave of research interest and produced numerous studies. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the current state of research in CF by mapping out its evolution and expecting future research directions from existing bodies of work. In doing so, we will examine key milestones and discuss potential areas of inquiry from a forward-looking perspective.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the level of active regions on HARPS-N stars and observed indicators' intensities increase with area and number of active regions. Notably, we saw variations in P21 (4.10 microns) and P23 (4.31 micron) with a 1-day period, coinciding with solar rotation. These patterns have potential as activity indicators and may be used to detect and characterize a planet's Doppler signal more accurately.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, the tunneling rate at high temperatures in the normal lead should be significantly lower (once again, a constant factor applies) for a Majorana peak to be detectable, thereby facilitating differentiation between the two cases through experimental identification of this relationship.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological quantum field theories. Shadow theory is characterized by a collection of structural properties, including functoriality, Morita invariance, and incorporation of compact objects, all of which are embodied in relationships between categories of shadows and compact shadows. This framework is sufficiently flexible to encompass various existing quantum field theory formulations and provides a natural environment for topological field theory segmentation. The Segal Conjecture and Dolgus' Homotopy Invariance are both naturally derived from shadow theory principles.

Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability, aiming for a straightforward solution. In contrast, our research aims to harness style-specific information extracted from professional color grading datasets to create various, artistically valid versions of an edited image. To achieve this, we employ a novel application of clustering on embedding spaces and assess its effectiveness through analysis of natural images.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where participants faced significant difficulties in processing multi-step instructions and varied video samples. To overcome these challenges, we developed an advanced feature fusion framework, integrating optical flow and frame features with instruction-guided video encoding. Our proposed method not only enhances feature representation but also effectively extracts vital information from video sequences. Additionally, we developed a learning strategy to seamlessly integrate video features with instruction-driven semantics. Our results demonstrate the outstanding performance of this approach in addressing the complex problem of video understanding with multiple steps and variable video samples.

This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the dynamics of snow crystals as they fall through air currents. Using a polarized camera, the team captures polarized reflected light from falling snow, enabling the identification of vortex structures through which the snow crystals move. As they traverse these currents, the snow crystals' orientations change, reflecting their interaction with turbulent flow dynamics. By correlating the snow's optical properties with the underlying atmospheric turbulence, the researchers uncover the link between vortex structures and the development of irregular, porous snow layers. Such structures compromise the snow's ability to insulate, affecting its temperature and density. Consequently, the snow's thermal conductivity is significantly increased, particularly at depths of 1-10 cm where the snow's porous nature is most pronounced.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite its significance in cognitive neuroscience, the theory's practical applications are limited due to its complex probabilistic framework. This research aims to bridge this gap by developing a novel reinforcement learning method inspired by active inference. The core idea is that an agent seeks to reduce uncertainty about the state of the environment to achieve rewards. This approach leads to a novel policy gradient algorithm that doesn't require a detailed model of the environment. Instead, the algorithm relies solely on the agent's current knowledge. When combined with a layered learning strategy, the method demonstrates sustained performance in complex Markov decision processes. Experimental results show that it outperforms leading reinforcement learning algorithms, including Proximal Policy Optimization.

In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a substantial hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression models to these data types tends to be unfeasible due to storage and computation constraints. The focus of our research is on an end-to-end sparsity through depth approach, combining specialized loss functions and data normalization techniques to efficiently handle 3D data volumes directly. The methodology was thoroughly evaluated by comparing its effects on different types of data and various numbers of zero-filled layers in VGG-like networks, revealing an impressive decline in both the total error and the error related to the non-zero pixels as the model progresses. Moreover, our approach proves capable of reducing data volume while preserving key features, thereby demonstrating its potential to effectively decompose large 3D data sets and facilitate real-time data reduction in scientific applications.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing our results with standard Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution functions for both the Newtonian and Finzi scenarios.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from fully embedded k-sizes of convex polygons in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs where the elements are numbered, and investigate a particular instance: determining if there exists a maximum-weight subset of elements in a given cgh that adheres to a given number of element limit. This problem is further categorized into two scenarios, each with either equal or non-equal element values. After conducting computational complexity assessments for both scenarios under different general geometric hypergraph settings, the study finds that one scenario remains an open question in terms of efficiency and whether it can be solved efficiently, while the other is proven to be an efficiently solvable problem. However, a specific instance with equal element values is shown to be an efficiently solvable problem.

To investigate the relative strengths of direct $\alpha$ decay and compound nuclear $\alpha$ decay, a detailed analysis is conducted across a wide range of target nuclei from $^{42}$Si to $^{100}$Mo, encompassing both ground-state and excited-state targets and a vast range of energy releases from -6 to 13 MeV. The study relies on a consistent set of empirical rules and a well-established decay model, requiring no adjustments or exceptions throughout. The results reveal that from stable or half-stable targets and for energy releases up to 3 MeV, the contribution of the direct and compound nuclear pathways is approximately equal. At higher energy releases, compound nuclear decay prevails, while in cases involving excited-state targets and lower energy releases, direct decay holds a higher relative strength. The findings are validated by comparisons with existing experimental data and by predicting previously unmeasured $\alpha$-decay half-lives with good accuracy.

A dynamic climbing strategy inspired by the lamprey's eversible head, allowing a robot to navigate complex terrain by expanding its height while maintaining foothold stability, has been developed. The authors present Trident, a robot designed to implement this strategy, which effectively climbs steep surfaces covered with artificial turf commonly found in manufacturing and logistics settings. By inflating a pair of flexible chambers in its head, the robot can extend its height, creating a pressure gradient that helps it maintain traction and navigate upward. Through a series of tests, the authors demonstrate that the robot can achieve significant stride lengths while climbing at various heights, with the longest recorded stride being 252% of its body height. The authors also evaluate different control methods and find that a combination of local sensing and image recognition produces the best results, enabling the robot to scale the toughest surfaces. Finally, the authors provide insights into possible future improvements in the robot's climbing performance.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Analytically derived expressions demonstrate how the network's overall AoI and throughput are affected under complex spatio-temporal interference. Furthermore, a neural network is designed to learn an optimal mapping between geographical locations and scheduling parameters under a random policy, eliminating the need for Channel State Information (CSI) after training. Experimental results show that the proposed schedule achieves higher throughput and a significantly lower AoI compared to existing scheduling methods.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations. We demonstrate that the solutions obtained can be represented through the use of a nonlinear spectral problem, whose spectral parameter variations are freely accessible. This spectral problem was initially developed in a paper by P. Cl\'ement, P. A. Clarkson, and N. M. Wood, with connections identified to a known set of non-linear equations from the integrable DSII context. Furthermore, the research in this field suggests computing the reflection coefficient as the spectral parameter varies, which in the absence of interactions would behave as a free particle. This analysis has the potential to quantify features such as spectral emission and shifts in spectral behavior that have been observed in experiments and numerical computations for two-dimensional scattering studies.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
including higher-order effects of gravitational wave radiation, reveal that late-time
eccentricities of inspiraling binaries are typically underestimated by standard
models by up to 30 percent for heavy systems like 300-solar-mass binaries at
10 Hz, and less so for lighter binaries. By incorporating more refined equations,
a novel, accurate analytic formula for eccentricities at late times is formulated.
Furthermore, this model's results remain largely insensitive to the masses of the
binary components, with deviations below two percent, and generalizes previous
work by Peters and Mathews.

A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and inverse Compton scattering (ICS) to create a pioneering X-ray source. By harnessing the capabilities of the Higgs boson factory's undulator-based XFELO and pairing it with the high-power electron beam of the SRF linac, this concept aims to generate extremely stable, coherent X-ray pulses at an unprecedented frequency of 4.17 Hz. To amplify these X-ray pulses, a novel ICS scheme is proposed, utilizing multiple uncorrelated photons from undulator radiation to create an enhanced light source. This innovative approach is expected to significantly increase the tuning range and flexibility of the XFELO, potentially expanding its application into in-vivo imaging and other fields.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems. Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes. To address these challenges, we propose a new approach, called DyGED, for recognizing events in evolving networks using a combination of temporal self-attention and structural awareness. Through extensive testing with diverse datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternative methods in accuracy, achieving up to a 7.5% improvement. The code for DyGED is available for public use at https://github.com/jay2019/DyGED

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and potential solutions identified, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. However, this method has its limitations, primarily due to the sampling error associated with examining only a small portion of the polyp, and the subjectivity of diagnosis, all of which increase the uncertainty in diagnosing polyps. In this research, we investigate the feasibility of quantifying the subjective uncertainty during diagnosis by applying Bayesian methods. By treating different regions of the histopathological analysis as hypotheses, we evaluate how the diagnosis changes as more analysis is performed, and how uncertainty is reduced. Furthermore, we demonstrate that uncertainty can sometimes be concurred upon across different doctors, and that incorporating this uncertainty may lead to better diagnostic accuracy.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source is represented by a letter $\mathcal{A}_i$ occurring with probability $p_i$, $i=1,\ldots,N$. This letter is conveyed to the adversary via a noisy channel $Q$, and the transmission rate $R$ is measured by the conditional entropy of the source given the received message. We establish the dependence of this conditional entropy on the probability distribution of the source letters $p_i$. This is achieved by introducing a metric called maximum min-entropy leakage, which quantifies a source encoder's security. This metric is further examined in the context of adversarial guessing and is compared with previous related approaches. It is shown that in the scenario of distinct source letters $p_i$, the maximum min-entropy leakage achieves its optimal value, equal to the error probability of the channel $Q$, and this leakage is assessed for various well-known channels, including the binary erasure channel, the binary symmetric channel and the memoryless binary arithmetic mean channel. Furthermore, our investigation encompasses source coding with a metric constraint. This problem involves finding an optimal source encoder such that any received message can be perfectly reconstructed and the average transmission rate satisfies a predetermined metric constraint. This source encoder is examined in the context of adversarial guessing and the associated leakage is analyzed. It is shown that in the scenario of adversarial guessing, the associated leakage is examined and it is proven

Deep learning-based generative models, specifically CNN-based VAEs and GANs, are being explored for generating high-dimensional medical images and then using those generated images to create real-world x-ray images from limited measurements, overcoming limitations in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. This study employs generative models to create synthetic fMRI data and utilizes it for reconstructions of actual fMRI data with varying levels of noise and deletion of voxels. Results show significant improvements over current methods in voxel value accuracy and image quality, as measured by PSNR and SSIM scores.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework is thoroughly tested using a challenging traveling salesman problem instance, where the Bayesian approach results in comparable high-quality approximate solutions while drastically decreasing computation costs.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. This approach can also be extended to calculate the area between an ellipse and a secant line, as well as the area between two secant lines. Several mathematical formulas have been developed to accomplish this, including expressions for the area of the overlap between two general ellipses, and simplified formulas applicable when one or both of the ellipses are reduced to circles. Additionally, formulas have been derived for calculating the area between an ellipse and a secant line, and the area between two secant lines. These formulas require only a simple and efficient computation of points of intersection, which can be achieved using a novel and efficient method. This method is inherently able to handle all four possible cases of intersection points (none, one, two, or four points) and has been optimized for performance. Furthermore, the proposed approach has been demonstrated to be accurate to double-precision errors when tested with a variety of test cases.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. The NTRL algorithm is developed to estimate the q-function, which is shown to be in direct relation to the instantaneous advantage rate function. The analysis includes assessment of the estimated q-function's bias and variance characteristics. Theoretical findings are substantiated through experimental validation in a Markov property-free setting, demonstrating that sampling variance significantly influences q-function estimation.

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but it's challenging to make predictions, especially for complex models with extensive magnetic patterns. We investigated the long-wavelength magnetic excitations of the triangular lattice Hubbard model, employing a combination of high-order diagrammatic approaches and advanced numerical methods with a neural network. Our results show that at low temperatures, the model exhibits a unique, gapped phase with gapped pockets surrounding a stable hot spot and Langer landau Fermi surface at optimal doping. However, the model has an unusual property where it can create extra symmetry-breaking U(1) spin zero modes at finite wave vectors, affecting the long-wavelength magnetic excitations and making the model in a long-wavelength long-wavelength magnetic excitation unstable. We discovered that by incorporating these zero modes into the simulation, the model exhibits a strange, flat region in its dynamical structure calculation at low temperatures. We further found that at high temperatures, the model demonstrates a Charle's law violation in its dynamical structure calculation and displays self-similarity behavior similar to that of a deconfined deacon, assuming a $SU(2)$ flavor symmetry.

Vertebral localization and identification are crucial for diagnosing and treating various spinal disorders. While significant advancements have been made in this area, certain clinical pathologies such as vertebral deformation and instrument artifact pose a challenge to accurate identification. To address this limitation, a novel and accurate method is presented for vertebral location and identification in the lumbar and cervical spine regions. This approach combines probabilistic neural networks to enhance image encoding and vertebrae identification, utilizing as-of-yet unpublisched CT scan data to establish a comprehensive and diverse dataset. Compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance on multiple datasets, showcasing its robustness and general applicability.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. This study applies the mathematical and topological properties of Markovian models to demonstrate the gauge invariance of the normalized cumulant-generating function. By utilizing the Hodge decomposition theorem, we break down the anti-symmetric transition measure down into its harmonic, co-Harmonic, and cyclic components. The normalized cumulant is then deconstructed from the generating function, and its generating function is shown to be invariance to arbitrary unitary transformations and topological deformations of the network.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for materials of any shape or orientation and can be determined experimentally through measurement of surface properties. Furthermore, we analyzed the optimal energy transfer between identical zinc oxide crystals for various orientations and found a significant number of conditions that facilitate this energy transfer.

We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates within high-quality microcavities at room temperature. By strategically modulating the non-resonant profile of the pump light, we can create and control an excitonic reservoir essential for polariton ordering. This advanced degree of freedom allows us to modulate the condensate on a millisecond timescale, where we can observe a tension between exciton-polariton boasonance and reservoir-induced instability. By activating brief pulses of pump light, we can pause the flow of pump particles, leading to a temporary cessation of the condensate. This technique grants us control over polariton populations on a millisecond timescale, offering a new approach to optical manipulation of room-temperature polariton condensates.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process likely involving the planet's disintegration. Identifying the factors driving this disintegration process is crucial for understanding how K2-22b met its current fate. To investigate this, we employ a new method that utilizes radial velocity data to estimate the mass of the surrounding debris cloud. This cloud's mass is then compared to the estimated masses of other disintegrating exoplanets and potentially surviving planets. Utilizing stellar high-speed wind models, we predict that a significant portion of the debris cloud's mass should be attributed to the host star's wind. To validate these estimates, we conduct numerical simulations of the system's orbital dynamics. The results of these simulations are then validated through comparison with observational data, with the model successfully reproducing variations in the planet's disintegration pattern and aligning with estimated masses of 3.63 x 10^-6 M Jupiter within the dispersal radius of 50 Jupiter radii. The implications of this study are then considered for other disintegrating exoplanets and their potential evolutionary paths.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra optimization. Designed for.NET environments, Daany is carefully crafted for efficient performance. This paper outlines the underlying architecture and key functionality of the library, highlighting its major features. Daany seamlessly integrates with popular.NET tools and platforms, such as Python and R, through interoperability bridges like PyCQL and RSharp. With its extensive programming capabilities, Daany easily accommodates user-defined operations. The library is meticulously engineered for high-speed data processing, supporting both block-based and element-level computation methods. Daany also includes an interactive data browser for detailed analysis and machine learning model training. The library is openly available on GitHub, and the source code can be used freely.

Despite his reputation as a skilled experimenter, few have explored how Galileo's mathematical abilities influenced his experimental work. This paper examines the role of mathematics in Galileo's experimental methodology by analyzing his Lezione teoretiche (Theoretical Lessons) and Le opere incomplete (Incomplete Works). These sources reveal that Galileo developed a strong connection between experimentation and mathematical reasoning. This is evident in his selection of problems, choice of experimental techniques, and interpretation of results, all of which were shaped by mathematical considerations. This research highlights the importance of considering Galileo's mathematical skills as a key factor in understanding his experimental innovations.

The increasing popularity of Tsallis' thermodynamic framework is largely attributed to its capability to describe phenomena exhibiting anomalous thermal properties, which requires adherence to generalized thermal equilibrium. Our study focuses on examining non-Gaussian influences on Saha's ionization through the application of Tsallis statistics. We addressed this challenge by generalizing the number density of electrons and considered the constraints imposed by continuous distributions of electron densities, resulting in Derivative-Determined Equations. Our results demonstrate that, in contrast to the case involving Gaussian distributions, the application of non-Gaussian statistics leads to distinct distributions of electron densities without the necessity of temperature dependence. However, we identified a condition under which the generalized Saha equation aligns with the standard version, yielding consistent results. We further validated our approach by comparing the standard Saha equation with its generalized counterpart in diverse astrophysical environments. Our findings emphasize the significance of non-Gaussian statistics in understanding ionization processes and can guide researchers in selecting the most suitable thermal framework based on observational data.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed kinetic regions, and full kinetic Particle-in-Cell (PIC) models. The examination of magnetic island formation, ion dynamics, and electrostatic potential reveals a good agreement among the methods, particularly for the MHD-AEPIC model with large-sized kinetic boxes.

This document provides an overview of the CLEOPATRA system, which facilitates
connection between natural language processing experts and their digital assistants.
It offers a platform for knowledge sharing and helps experts manage their digital
assistants more effectively by providing relevant knowledge to address questions
raised during problem-solving tasks. A key strength of CLEOPATRA lies in its
ability to facilitate multi-turn conversations by uniting the expertise of
specialists through the integration of semantic roles. As a primary application,
the system has been fine-tuned for use by computer vision researchers and their
digital assistants, aligning with the requirements of current conversation AI
models. Its capabilities will likely benefit other research domains as well as
future human-AI collaboration platforms.
